0.title: Ezra: The God Who Rebuilds
0.overview:
The message. Ezra is the story of God keeping his word after his people had broken theirs. He had sent them into exile for their idolatry; now, just as his prophets had promised, he turns the heart of a pagan emperor and brings a remnant home to rebuild his house and to live again by his law. Opposition, delay and sin cannot undo what God has begun, because “the hand of the LORD” is on the work (7:6). Yet the book is honest that this is not yet the end of the story: the new temple is smaller than the old, the people still fall into the old sins, and David’s heir comes home without a throne. It leaves God’s people waiting for more.

Background: the world of the book. In 587 or 586 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon burned Solomon’s temple and carried Judah into exile. In 539 BC Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia, and in his first year as its king, about 538 BC, he issued the decree that opens the book (1:1–4). Persia’s kings ruled from India to Egypt and let conquered peoples go home and honour their own gods, so long as they paid tribute. Judah was now a small district of the province “Beyond the River”, west of the Euphrates. Some fifty thousand went back, servants included (2:64–65), to a ruined city among hostile neighbours.

Two stories, a lifetime apart. Chapters 1–6 run from about 538 to 515 BC. The first party returns under Zerubbabel, of David’s royal line, and Jeshua, also called Joshua the high priest. The work stops for some sixteen years after the foundation is laid, until the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir the people in 520 BC, and the temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius I, 516 or 515 BC (6:15). Then “Now after this” (7:1) passes over nearly sixty years, the years of Esther, to 458 BC, when Ezra himself arrives in the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (7:7). Thirteen years later Nehemiah came to rebuild the walls; in the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah were one book.

Background: the writer. The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition credits Ezra, and from 7:27 to the end of chapter 9 he speaks in the first person as in a memoir. The rest is told in the third person and quotes registers, inventories and Persian letters. Many scholars think a later editor, perhaps the Chronicler, compiled it; others think Ezra did. This commentary reads it as a faithful history built on Ezra’s own memoir and genuine documents, put together by Ezra or someone close to him not long after the events. Nothing in its message depends on knowing the compiler’s name.

How to read it. Ezra is history, written to be believed and learned from. The long lists are not filler: for families rebuilding their lives, a name in the register was a title deed. The order is not always by date: 4:6–23 gathers opposition from the later reigns of Xerxes and Artaxerxes to show a pattern, before 4:24 returns to the temple. The passages in 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26 are in Aramaic, the language of the Persian letters they quote.

When did Ezra come? The traditional date is 458 BC, in the reign of Artaxerxes I, before Nehemiah. Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, putting Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah. But the two men appear together at the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:9) and at the dedication of the wall (Nehemiah 12:26, 36). This commentary’s view is that the traditional date is the most natural reading, and that nothing in the book’s message depends on settling it.

How the book makes its case. The book tells of two rebuildings: first the house of God [1–6], then the people of God by the word of God [7–10]. God stirs Cyrus and the families who go home, and the register names them [1–2]. They build the altar, then lay the foundation, and the old men who remembered Solomon’s temple weep while the young shout for joy [3]. Enemies frighten them and write to the king, and the work stops [4]. Preaching starts it again; Darius finds Cyrus’s decree in the archives, and the house is finished with a Passover kept in joy, “for the LORD had made them joyful” (6:22) [5–6]. Then Ezra, priest and “a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses” (7:6), comes because he “had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (7:10) [7]. He travels without soldiers, trusting the good hand of God [8]. Finding the people married into idol-worshipping households, he prays a confession that asks for nothing [9]. The people make a covenant to put away those marriages [10].

The hardest chapter. Many readers are troubled by chapter 10, where men put away foreign wives and their children. Some read it as costly zeal, others as harsh or even racial. This commentary’s view is that it was about worship, not race: the law forbade these marriages because they would turn hearts to other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4); Ruth the Moabite became David’s great-grandmother; and anyone who “separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD” was welcome at the Passover (6:21). The measure belonged to one perilous moment, when the small remnant holding the promise of the Messiah’s line was sliding back into the idolatry it had been exiled for. It is recorded, not prescribed for the church. For Christians the apostle answers plainly: “if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her” (1 Corinthians 7:12).

Where it leads: to Christ. Ezra points to Christ by promise, pattern and need. By promise: Zerubbabel stands in both genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27), so David’s line came home from exile still waiting for its King. By pattern: the temple was where God dwelt among his people and sin was atoned for. Haggai promised that “the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9), and it was, when the Son of God walked into it. Yet he spoke of a greater temple still: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), and “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). Ezra’s prayer, confessing “our iniquities” (9:6) though he had not shared the sin, is a glimpse of the one Priest who bore sins that were not his own. And by need: within a generation the same marriages were back (Nehemiah 13:23–27). A law in the hand could not change the heart. Ezra leaves us longing for the new covenant God promised, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), which Christ sealed with his blood.

For us. Ezra speaks to Christians who feel small, opposed and slow. God keeps his promises on his own timetable, and he rules the rulers of the world for his people’s good. Stalled work is restarted by his word preached, not by better plans. Every Christian is called, like Ezra, to study the Scriptures, to do them and to teach them, in that order. And when we find the old sins back in our lives, Ezra shows the way home: honest confession, with hope. As Shecaniah said, “even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this” (10:2). Our hope does not rest on our reforms, but on the God who has not forsaken his people (9:9), and who has given us a better temple, a greater Priest, and a King on David’s throne for ever.

1.title: The Stirred Heart: Cyrus, the Decree, and the Upward Call
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.<sup>3</sup>Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."<sup>5</sup>Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.<sup>7</sup>Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods.<sup>8</sup>Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.<sup>9</sup>And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers,<sup>10</sup>30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels;<sup>11</sup>all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the book’s first page, and it picks up exactly where 2 Chronicles broke off. Jerusalem and its temple have lain in ruins for about fifty years, Judah has been in exile in Babylon, and Babylon itself has just fallen to Cyrus of Persia (see the introduction).

The message. God keeps his word, and he moves both emperors and ordinary hearts to do it. The return from exile did not happen because Persia had a generous policy, but because the LORD had promised it through Jeremiah and then stirred up the spirit of Cyrus and the spirits of his own people. Nothing that belonged to God’s house was lost in Babylon, and nothing will be.

Why it was said. The first readers were the small, poor community that had come home, or their children. They had every reason to wonder whether God was still with them and whether their humble beginnings counted for anything (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that their return began in heaven, not in the Persian court.

How the chapter makes its case. The LORD stirs Cyrus to fulfil Jeremiah’s word, and Cyrus decrees that the house of God be rebuilt, that any of God’s people may go, and that those who stay must help (vv. 1–4). The same verb is used again for the families: “everyone whose spirit God had stirred” rises to go, loaded with their neighbours’ gifts, as Israel once left Egypt (vv. 5–6). Then the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar carried off are brought out of a pagan temple, counted, and handed to Sheshbazzar to take home (vv. 7–11).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The chapter is a promise kept to the letter, and Paul says that all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Isaiah had even called Cyrus the LORD’s “anointed” (Isaiah 45:1): a pagan king used once to set captives free and build God’s house, foreshadowing the true Anointed One, who sets sinners free from a far worse captivity and builds a living temple. And the counted vessels picture the Good Shepherd, who will “lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39).

For us. If God could move a Persian emperor’s pen, he can rule the forces that seem to run your life. If you have turned back to God, thank him for stirring your heart, for that was his work. And whether you go or stay, you have a part in his work, as the neighbours who loaded the carts did.
1.theology:
The chapter is built on one verb used twice: the LORD stirred up Cyrus (v. 1), and God stirred the families who went (v. 5). Neither the emperor's decree nor the exiles' decision is the first cause of the return; God is. Isaiah even calls Cyrus the LORD's anointed (Isa 45:1), a pagan king used for one task: he opened a road home from Babylon. The Anointed One, the Christ, opens the way home from a deeper exile, sin and death, and brings his people not to a ruined city but to God (1 Pet 3:18).

The return is written as a second exodus: a people leaving a foreign land with their neighbours' silver and gold, carrying the holy things, going up to the place of God's presence.
1.examples:
An emperor's permission opened the road, and it still took God stirring each family before anyone sold a house and started walking. Those who stayed in Babylon were not condemned; they loaded the carts of the ones who went.

The cups Belshazzar drank from on the night Babylon fell were counted out by a Persian treasurer and carried back to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The LORD Stirred Up the Spirit of Cyrus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word, and he does it by moving the most powerful man on earth. Verse 1 gives the real reason for the return before it gives the decree: the LORD stirred up Cyrus so that Jeremiah’s prophecy would be fulfilled. Cyrus then proclaims that the God of heaven has given him his kingdoms and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem (v. 2). Any of God’s people may go up and rebuild it (v. 3), and those who stay are to help them with silver, gold, goods and animals, besides gifts for the house of God (v. 4). Policy and providence are both at work, and the text says plainly which one is in charge.
verseByVerse.theology: The first three verses of Ezra are the last two verses of 2 Chronicles, almost word for word, and verse 1 says at once why the return happened: to fulfil the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah had named this king before he was born: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose (Isa 44:28). And Jeremiah had put a number on the exile, seventy years (Jer 25:11; 29:10). Verse 1 names Jeremiah's word, and Isaiah's was fulfilled in the same decree, in the mouth of a Persian who, as far as we know, had never read either. Because Isaiah names Cyrus so exactly, many modern scholars date Isaiah 40-55 to the exile; this commentary follows the traditional view, since the New Testament quotes those chapters as Isaiah's (John 12:38-41) and their argument is that God declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The return from exile happened because the LORD had promised it through Jeremiah and then moved the heart of the emperor to make it happen. Cyrus decrees that God’s house be rebuilt, lets any of God’s people go, and orders those who stay to pay for it.

Where Chronicles stops. A reader coming straight from 2 Chronicles has read this before. Chronicles stops in the middle of Cyrus’s proclamation, on “Let him go up” (2 Chronicles 36:23), and Ezra finishes the sentence: “and rebuild the house of the LORD”. The join is meant to be seen: the exile was not the end of the story but a sentence not yet completed.

That the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled. Verse 1 tells us why it happened before it tells us what happened. Not because Persia had a policy of resettling conquered peoples, though it did, nor because Cyrus was generous, but to fulfil what Jeremiah had said about seventy years while Jerusalem still stood and nobody believed him.

The LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus. Cyrus left a clay cylinder, which still exists, crediting his conquest of Babylon to the god Marduk. The Bible does not argue with his inscription; it simply tells us who was actually moving him. A man can be the instrument of a God he has never known, and his own account of his motives is not the last word. Isaiah had said the same of him by name: “I have stirred him up in righteousness … he shall build my city and set my exiles free” (Isaiah 45:13).

Whoever is among you of all his people. The decree has two halves: whoever wants to go, let him go, and whoever stays, let him help. “Survivor” (v. 4) is the word for the exiles now, the ones who came through, and the emperor writes the return and its funding into the same order.

Who really moves history? We tend to explain history as Cyrus’s own officials would have: by policy, economics and power, and to assume that once we have found the political cause we have found the only one. Ezra declines to choose: the return had a Persian policy behind it, and the LORD behind the policy. Scripture does this nowhere more sharply than at the cross. Pilate and the priests had their reasons; yet the apostles prayed that Herod and Pilate had gathered “to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). If God can work through an emperor’s foreign policy and through the worst injustice ever done, he can work through the forces that seem to run your life. They are real, and they are not in charge.

Were Jeremiah’s seventy years fulfilled? Counted from the first deportation in about 605 BC to the return in about 538 BC, they come to some sixty-seven years, a round seventy covering Babylon’s dominion, as Jeremiah said (Jeremiah 29:10). Scripture also counts them another way, from the burning of the temple in 587 or 586 to its rebuilding in about 516 (Zechariah 1:12). Either way, the number God named was kept.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let exiled peoples go home. Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew Bible, covering about a century of return and rebuilding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Everyone Whose Spirit God Had Stirred
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who stirred the emperor also stirs his people, and he loses nothing that is his. Not everyone went home, but “everyone whose spirit God had stirred” rose up to go, and their neighbours loaded them with gifts, as Israel once left Egypt carrying the wealth of its neighbours (vv. 5–6). Then Cyrus brings out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken as trophies, and his treasurer counts them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, who carries them home with the exiles (vv. 7–11). Every bowl is listed, because nothing belonging to God’s house was left behind in Babylon.
verseByVerse.theology: God stirred the spirit of the most powerful man on earth, and the spirits of ordinary families in Babylon. A decree can open a road, and only God can make anybody want to walk down it.
verseByVerse.examples: The inventory is careful enough to keep two figures that do not obviously agree (vv. 9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem. And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stirred ordinary families as surely as he stirred the emperor, and those who stayed behind were stirred to give. A decree opened the door; God moved people to walk through it.

Everyone whose spirit God had stirred. This repeats the verb of verse 1, and the repetition is the chapter’s main point: God moved the emperor and the families alike.

To go up to rebuild the house of the LORD. A permission moves nobody. Families born in Babylon, with houses, trades and grandparents buried there, had to decide to sell up and walk some nine hundred miles to a city most of them had never seen, which was a ruin. What got them onto the road was the same hand that got Cyrus to pick up his pen.

All who were about them aided them. Not everyone went, and the text does not condemn those who stayed; Jeremiah had told the exiles to build houses and seek the welfare of the city (Jeremiah 29:5–7). What it records is what those who stayed did for those who went: silver, gold, goods and animals, besides freewill offerings.

A second exodus. Israel left Egypt carrying its neighbours’ valuables too (Exodus 12:35–36). A second exodus has begun, and it starts the way the first one did. Both point to the greater rescue Christ accomplished, when he brought his people out of the slavery of sin through his death and resurrection.

The pattern of every return. Providence opens doors: a decree, a circumstance, a chance. But nobody goes through a door because it is open. They go because something has been stirred in them, and the Bible never lets us take the credit for that part. If you have come back to God, he stirred you first. And some are stirred to go, and some to load the cart: those who give so that others can go are part of the same work.

verseByVerse.quote: Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods. Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken as trophies were counted out to the last bowl and carried home. Nothing that belonged to God’s house was written off as lost to Babylon.

That Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem. Anyone who has just finished 2 Chronicles watched the vessels go, in three loads (2 Chronicles 36:7, 10, 18). Nebuchadnezzar set them in his own temple as trophies, the tableware of a God he thought he had beaten, and on the last night of Babylon Belshazzar drank wine from them and praised gods of gold and silver while a hand wrote on the wall (Daniel 5:2–5).

Counted them out to Sheshbazzar. Now they come out counted: a named official on one side, a named recipient on the other, and a list between them. It is the same care with holy things that sent two men to empty Joash’s chest together (2 Chronicles 24:11).

All the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. The items listed add up to 2,499, while verse 11 gives the whole as 5,400. The text does not explain the gap, and it is better to say so. The likeliest reading is that the list names the principal pieces and the total counts everything that went back. Numbers were also easily miscopied by hand. Nothing in the chapter turns on the discrepancy; what turns on the verse is that somebody counted.

Nothing written off as lost. That is how the Lord Jesus speaks of the people his Father has given him: “this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). The vessels were counted out of Babylon to the last bowl. He counts his people the same way, and none of them is left behind in the house of another god.

Who was Sheshbazzar? He hands over the vessels here and then all but vanishes. Chapter 5 says he laid the foundations of the house (5:16); chapter 3 says Zerubbabel did (3:8–10). Some take them for one man with a Babylonian name and a Hebrew one; others for two leaders in succession, Sheshbazzar the first governor and Zerubbabel the man who led the work. The text leaves it open, and so should we.

Uncertain wording. Several words in the inventory are rare and their exact meaning is not known. The word translated “censers” (v. 9) occurs only here; older versions guessed “knives”, and others suggest pans or some other temple utensil. In verse 10 the Hebrew adds a word after “bowls of silver” that may mean “of a second kind” or “duplicates”. What is clear is that these were the vessels of the house of God, listed piece by piece.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshbazzar may be another name for Zerubbabel, or an earlier governor.

keyVerse.quote: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia
keyVerse.note: The whole book rests on this sentence. Before we hear the emperor’s decree we are told whose word it fulfils and whose hand is moving him, so that the return is seen as God keeping his promise, not as Persian policy. The same verb, “stirred”, then explains why ordinary families went (v. 5).

1.reflection:
Verse 1 says the return happened “that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled”, and that the LORD stirred up a pagan emperor. Where are you tempted to explain events in your life or the world only by politics, money or chance? What difference does it make that God rules over them?

God stirred both Cyrus and the families who went home (vv. 1, 5). If you have come to God or come back to him, what part did God’s stirring play? How should that shape the way we pray for people who seem far from him?

Some went, and some stayed and gave (vv. 4, 6). In the work of the gospel today, who are the goers and who are the givers, and where is God calling you to stand?

Every vessel taken to Babylon was counted and brought home (vv. 9–11), and Jesus said he would lose nothing of all the Father had given him (John 6:39). How does that promise comfort a believer who feels forgotten or lost?

2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with the temple vessels leaving Babylon “when the exiles were brought up” (1:11). Chapter 2 tells us who those exiles were: the register of the families who made the journey home, with their leaders, their priests and servants, and what they gave when they arrived.

The message. God brought his people home by name. The exile had threatened to dissolve Israel into Babylon as every other conquered nation dissolved, and this list is God’s answer: family by family, town by town, the people survived, because he kept them. To be on this list was to belong to the people of the promise, and the chapter treats that belonging as precious.

Why it was said. For families rebuilding their lives in a ruined land, a name in the register was a title deed and a place among God’s people (see the introduction). The list told the first readers who they were, and its careful honesty about those who could not prove their descent told them how seriously God’s worship was to be guarded.

How the chapter makes its case. Eleven leaders head the list, Zerubbabel of David’s line and Jeshua the high priest first (vv. 1–2). The lay families are counted by clan and by town, Bethlehem and Anathoth among them (vv. 3–35). Then come the many priests and the few Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants (vv. 36–58). Some could not prove their descent; they came anyway, but priests missing from the register were kept from the altar until God should give a decision (vv. 59–63). The whole assembly is totalled, animals and all, and the families give generously to rebuild the house on its old site before going home to their towns (vv. 64–70).

Where it leads. By promise and by the need it exposes. Zerubbabel, at the head of the list, stands in both genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27), and the hundred and twenty-three men of Bethlehem went home to the town where the Ruler would be born (Micah 5:2). The priests who could not find their names show the limits of a priesthood that rests on a written pedigree; Jesus is a priest “by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16). And a roll of God’s people points to the names written in heaven (Luke 10:20).

For us. God knows his people one by one, and no one who belongs to him is lost in the crowd. Your standing with him does not rest on a record you must keep or prove, but on Christ, who holds it for you. Like these families, give to his work gladly and according to your ability, even before you see what it will become.
2.theology:
The list is the answer to the exile's question: whether Israel would survive as a people or melt into Babylon. God had not preserved an idea of Israel; he had preserved named families.

Verses 59-63 hold law and mercy together. The standard for the priesthood is not relaxed, and nobody is thrown out of the people; the arrangement waits for a word from God, and in the end for a Priest of a different kind.
2.examples: A family called the sons of Sisera came home to serve at the altar, and a priest's descendants, who had taken the name of a famous father-in-law, could no longer find themselves in the register. The first thing the families did on reaching the ruins was give money toward a building that was not there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–35 — The Men of the People of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God brought his people home family by family, and he had their names written down. The list begins with the people “each to his own town” and the eleven leaders who brought them, headed by Zerubbabel, heir of David, and Jeshua, the high priest (vv. 1–2). Then it counts the lay families, first by the name of their clan (vv. 3–20), then by the name of their town (vv. 21–35). Bethlehem, Anathoth, Bethel and Ai are all there. For a people who had nearly vanished into Babylon, every line was evidence that God had kept them and that his promises to the land still stood.
verseByVerse.theology: The list is not an interruption of the story; it is the evidence the story needed. Half a century and more after the deportations these families could still tell you who their great-grandfather was and which village he farmed. God had kept the sons of Parosh.
verseByVerse.examples: Read the town names slowly: some of them carry promises made before the exile, and the men walking home to them are the promises kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried captive to Babylonia. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the people who came home from exile, each to his own town, led by the heir of David and the high priest.

Each to his own town. Fifty to seventy years after the deportations, these families still knew which town was theirs, though most had never seen it. And they came back as “people of the province”: Judah was no longer a kingdom with a son of David on its throne, only a small district of the Persian empire.

They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua. Eleven leaders are named, Zerubbabel and Jeshua at their head: the heir of David and the high priest, the two offices the community will be rebuilt around (see Joshua the high priest). Nehemiah’s copy of the same list has twelve names (Nehemiah 7:7), and twelve is probably the point: a returning Israel led by one man for each tribe. Somewhere in the copying of Ezra’s list, one name has probably dropped out.

Nehemiah … Mordecai. These are not the famous men of those names. The Mordecai of the book of Esther and the Nehemiah who rebuilt the walls were active decades later, in the 480s and the 440s BC. These are other men who shared the names.

Why the Bible keeps lists. Every name answered the question the exile had raised: would Israel survive as a people or melt into Babylon as other conquered nations had? And the heir of David at its head was the ancestor of a greater Son of David (Matthew 1:12), so the promise of the King came home with him.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 775. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,812. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 945. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Bani, 642. The sons of Bebai, 623. The sons of Azgad, 1,222. The sons of Adonikam, 666. The sons of Bigvai, 2,056. The sons of Adin, 454. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Bezai, 323. The sons of Jorah, 112. The sons of Hashum, 223. The sons of Gibbar, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighteen families were counted by name, and God cared about each of them down to the last man.

Family by family. Eighteen family groups, 15,604 men: some came home two thousand strong, some fewer than a hundred, and behind each figure lies a decision about who went and who stayed. Somebody kept these records through generations in a foreign country, and that is itself a kind of faith. A family that goes on writing down its descent in exile expects to go home.

The sons of Zattu, 945. God did not rescue his people in the abstract. He rescued the sons of Zattu, nine hundred and forty-five of them, and had it written down. The Good Shepherd still “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3).

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? The list in Nehemiah 7 differs in places. Nehemiah copied the old register (Nehemiah 7:5) and may have updated it; the lists may count slightly different things, and numbers were easily miscopied. None of this touches what the passage teaches, and a copyist’s slip in a figure does not unsettle the trustworthiness of what God has said: this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Bethlehem, 123. The men of Netophah, 56. The men of Anathoth, 128. The sons of Azmaveth, 42. The sons of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The sons of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 223. The sons of Nebo, 52. The sons of Magbish, 156. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Senaah, 3,630.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifteen towns sent their sons home, and among them were places that carried God’s promises.

Town by town. Now the counting changes from the name of a family to the name of a town: fifteen entries, 8,540 men. The largest group is the last: Senaah, 3,630, a place otherwise almost unknown.

The sons of Bethlehem, 123. Bethlehem sends a hundred and twenty-three back to David’s town, where Micah had said a ruler would come from (Micah 5:2). Five centuries later Herod’s scribes read that verse to the wise men, and the Ruler had been born there (Matthew 2:5–6). The hundred and twenty-three were keeping the town alive for him.

The men of Anathoth, 128. Anathoth was Jeremiah’s town (Jeremiah 1:1). During the last siege God told him to buy a field there, before witnesses, as a pledge: “Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land” (Jeremiah 32:15). Here are a hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth walking home to farm it. God’s promises are kept down to the field.

The men of Bethel and Ai, 223. Bethel, where Jeroboam set up his golden calf, and Ai, where Israel lost its first battle because of Achan’s theft, are on the list too. The people coming home to places with such histories are not asked to account for them: God’s mercy does not wait for a clean past.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–63 — Priests, Levites, and Those Who Could Not Prove It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people who served God’s house came home too, and its holiness was guarded with care. Many priests returned (vv. 36–39), but only a handful of Levites, with the singers and gatekeepers (vv. 40–42), and a long roll of temple servants and the sons of Solomon’s servants (vv. 43–58). Then the register is honest about those it could not confirm. Some families could not prove they were Israelites, and came anyway (vv. 59–60). Some priests could not find their names, and were kept from the altar and the most holy food until a priest could ask God for a decision by the Urim and Thummim (vv. 61–63).
verseByVerse.theology: The priests who could not prove their descent were not expelled from the people. They were barred from the priesthood and told to wait for a word from God.
verseByVerse.examples: Compare the numbers of priests and Levites: about fifty-eight to one.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The families of the altar came home in large numbers, because the whole return was organised around the worship of God.

The priests. Four priestly families came, 4,289 men, roughly one in seven on the list. The return was organised around worship, and without the altar the rest made no sense.

The sons of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua. The first family is “of the house of Jeshua”, the high priest of verse 2. The line of Aaron has come through the exile unbroken, its head beside the heir of David. Both offices point beyond themselves: Zechariah would later speak of “the man whose name is the Branch”, who would build the temple and be “a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:12–13), King and Priest in one person, fulfilled in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the sons of Hodaviah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 128. The sons of the gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, and the sons of Shobai, in all 139.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Very few Levites came home, because their service was the hardest and least honoured, and the shortage would last.

The Levites. Only seventy-four Levites came, though the temple system assumed they would far outnumber the priests. They did the heavy work of the house: carrying, cleaning, slaughtering and teaching (see Priests and Levites).

Why so few came. A Levite had no land to go back to, only hard work in a ruin, and the shortage lasted. When Ezra assembles his own caravan he finds “none of the sons of Levi” there (8:15). Humble service is always the hardest to fill, and Christ, who “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45), honours it most.

The singers: the sons of Asaph. The singers are the sons of Asaph, the guild David set apart for the music of the house, still singing after two generations in a country where their harps had hung on the willows (Psalm 137:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Siaha, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebanah, the sons of Hagabah, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hagab, the sons of Shamlai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Asnah, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephisim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazluth, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, and the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Hassophereth, the sons of Peruda, the sons of Jaalah, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and the sons of Ami. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple servants, many of them probably not Israelite by descent, came home to the house they had served, and they are counted with the rest.

The temple servants. The longest run of names in the chapter, and the most easily skipped.

Who they were. The temple servants (literally “given ones”) are often connected with the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made “cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD” (Joshua 9:27), and Solomon’s servants with the non-Israelite peoples he conscripted as labour (2 Chronicles 8:7–9). If that is right, many of these families were not Israelite by descent at all. Attached to the house of God for centuries, they went into exile with it and now came back to it.

The sons of Sisera. One name in the middle stops a reader: “the sons of Sisera” (v. 53). It is the name of Jabin’s general, the man Jael killed with a tent peg (Judges 4:21). Nothing says this family descended from him. But a family carrying the name of Israel’s old enemy is walking home from Babylon to serve at the altar of Israel’s God, and the list gives them a line of their own.

Counted with the rest. All of them together come to 392, and the book does not rank them below the priests. It is a small foretaste of the gospel, in which those who were “strangers to the covenants of promise” are made “members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:12, 19).

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, though they could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, and the sons of Nekoda, 652. Also, of the sons of the priests: the sons of Habaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, and the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but they were not found there, and so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food, until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who could not prove their descent came home anyway, but priests without a record were kept from the altar until God himself should decide.

They could not prove their fathers’ houses. Six hundred and fifty-two people who could not show they were Israelites came anyway, and nobody turned them back.

The sons of Barzillai. One priestly family has a story. Barzillai the Gileadite fed David at Mahanaim when he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 19:31–39). Generations later a priest married into that famous family and took its name, and his descendants could no longer be found in the priestly register under their own.

But they were not found there. One of the saddest sentences in the book, yet what was done was careful. They were not expelled from the people; they were kept from the priesthood and the most holy food until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots by which the high priest asked God for a decision. Nobody in authority would decide by sentiment, for the holiness of the altar mattered.

A wait that ended. For at least one family the waiting ended. Eighty years later the temple treasure was weighed into the hands of “Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah” (8:33), whose line Nehemiah gives as “the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz” (Nehemiah 3:4). The sons of Hakkoz, unregistered in 538, were serving as priests by 458. The text never tells us how.

A Priest of a different kind. They were waiting, without knowing it, for a Priest of a different kind. Hebrews says Jesus came from Judah, a tribe Moses never connected with the priesthood, and is a priest “not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16). The register that shut out the sons of Barzillai could not have admitted him either. His priesthood does not rest on a document that can be lost in a fire, and neither does the standing of anyone who comes to God through him.

The anxiety of the unprovable self. These families are closer to us than they look. Today identity has to be established and defended: by achievement, self-expression, the groups we join, the profiles we curate. All of it is a kind of register, and the fear underneath is the fear of verse 62: what if I search and am not found there? An identity that has to be proved can always be disproved, by a failure, a rejection, a lost document. The gospel offers a different standing. It rests not on a record we keep but on a word God has spoken: to all who received Christ, “he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). A self that has been given cannot be lost in a fire.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “governor” in verse 63 is a Persian title (tirshatha), probably meaning something like “His Excellency”; it is used of Nehemiah later (Nehemiah 8:9), and here probably of Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel. What exactly the Urim and Thummim were, and how they gave an answer, is not known; they were probably lots kept in the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:30).
verseByVerse.note: The Urim and Thummim, probably sacred lots kept in the high priest's breastpiece, were used to learn God’s will.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people who had come home gave first to the house of God. The total of the whole assembly is given, with servants, singers and animals, a picture of a whole people on the move (vv. 64–67). When they reached Jerusalem, some heads of families made freewill offerings so that the house could be built again on its old site, each giving according to his ability (vv. 68–69). Then everyone settled in his own town (v. 70). Before they had rebuilt their own houses, they gave for a building that did not yet exist.
verseByVerse.theology: They gave according to their ability: not a fixed sum from everyone but each in proportion to what he had, the measure Paul uses of the Macedonians (2 Cor 8:3). And they gave not to buy their way back into God's favour but because he had already brought them home; the gift followed the rescue.
verseByVerse.examples: The families had no house to give to, only a site, and they gave anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337, and they had 200 male and female singers. Their horses were 736, their mules were 245, their camels were 435, and their donkeys were 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly is totalled, with servants and animals: a whole people on the move.

The whole assembly together was 42,360. The figures in the list add up to 29,818, and the stated total is 12,542 higher. The heading counts “the men of the people of Israel” (v. 2), so the likeliest reading is that the grand total includes people the clan lists never itemised, perhaps women, or others whose families were not listed. Nehemiah’s copy has the same total and different details (Nehemiah 7:66). It is better to say so than to force the arithmetic.

Male and female singers. Not the temple singers of verse 41, but probably singers for feasts and funerals, like those who sang laments for Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:25).

Their donkeys were 6,720. More than eight thousand animals, most of them donkeys: what a column of families carrying everything they own over nine hundred miles actually looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the heads of families, when they came to the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site. According to their ability they gave to the treasury of the work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments. Now the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants lived in their towns, and all the rest of Israel in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before they had roofs over their own heads, the families gave generously to rebuild God’s house on its old foundations, each according to what he had.

Made freewill offerings for the house of God. The house of the LORD was a heap of burned stone, and the first thing these families did was give toward a building that was not there.

To erect it on its site. Not a fresh start on cleaner ground, but the rock where Solomon’s house had stood, where David had bought a threshing floor, and where Abraham had once taken his son (2 Chronicles 3:1; Genesis 22:2). The return was not a new religion. It was the old one, rebuilt on its own foundations.

According to their ability they gave. Each gave in proportion to what he had, as Paul describes the Macedonian churches, who gave “according to their means … and beyond their means” (2 Corinthians 8:3). God does not ask for what we do not have, but he delights in what is freely given.

All the rest of Israel in their towns. The chapter ends quietly. Seventy verses of names, and the last one sends everybody home to start ploughing.

Names written in heaven. A roll of names like this pictures something Jesus told his disciples to care about more than any success. When they came back exhilarated from their mission, he told them not to rejoice in what they had achieved, “but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Babylon could not blot out the sons of Parosh. Nothing can blot out a name he has written down.

Uncertain wording. The coins of verse 69 are not certain. The ESV’s “darics” were Persian gold coins; some think the Hebrew word means the Greek drachma instead, and which coin is meant is still debated. Either way the gift was large, and the parallel in Nehemiah gives somewhat different figures (Nehemiah 7:70–72).
verseByVerse.note: A daric was a gold coin of about 1/4 ounce and a mina about 1¼ pounds (ESV notes).

keyVerse.quote: Some of the heads of families, when they came to the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site.
keyVerse.note: After seventy verses of names, this verse shows what the list was for. The people God brought home by name gave first, and freely, to rebuild his house on its old foundations, before they had rebuilt their own. A people restored by grace responds with worship and generosity.

2.reflection:
Long lists of names are easy to skip. Why do you think God had this one written down and kept in Scripture? What does it tell you about how he regards his people one by one?

Some families could not prove their descent, and some priests could not find their names in the register (vv. 59–63). Where do people today look for a secure identity, and why does an identity that has to be proved always feel fragile? How does belonging to Christ change that?

Only seventy-four Levites came home, against more than four thousand priests (vv. 36–40). Why is humble, unseen service so often the hardest to fill, and how does Jesus’ example speak to that in your church?

The families gave to God’s house “according to their ability” before they had rebuilt their own homes (vv. 68–69). What would it look like for you to put God’s work first in your giving, and what holds you back?

3.title: The Altar Before the Temple: Worship, Weeping, and the Shout of Joy
3.text: <sup>1</sup>When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God.<sup>3</sup>They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.<sup>4</sup>And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required,<sup>5</sup>and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid.<sup>7</sup>So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.<sup>8</sup>Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers.<sup>10</sup>And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.<sup>12</sup>But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy,<sup>13</sup>so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
3.overview:
Where we are. The families listed in chapter 2 have settled in their towns. Now, a few months after their return, they gather in Jerusalem to begin the work they came for.

The message. Worship comes first, and God’s steadfast love does not depend on the size of the building. Before walls or temple, the frightened people build an altar and offer sacrifice as God’s law commands. When the foundation is laid, they sing the old song of the LORD’s goodness and unending love “toward Israel”, the very people he had sent into exile. Grief for what was lost and joy for what God is doing rise together, and both are honest.

Why it was said. The first readers lived with a temple far smaller than Solomon’s, in a land surrounded by hostile neighbours (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that God was truly among them, and that neither their fear nor their small beginnings could stop his love.

How the chapter makes its case. In the holy seventh month the people gather “as one man” and build the altar on its old site, “for fear was on them”, and the daily offerings begin again (vv. 1–3). They keep the Feast of Booths and the calendar of sacrifice, and order cedar as Solomon did (vv. 4–7). In the second year the work begins under the Levites, and at the laying of the foundation the singers praise the LORD: “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel” (vv. 8–11). The old men who had seen Solomon’s house weep, the young shout for joy, and the two sounds cannot be told apart (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The altar came first because sinners can only meet God through sacrifice, and every offering on it pointed to the one sacrifice Christ would make “for all time” (Hebrews 10:12). The old men wept over a smaller house, but Haggai promised that “the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9), and it was, because the Son of God walked into it. In him the steadfast love they sang reached its height, for “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

For us. When you are afraid, go first to God through Christ, the better altar, rather than waiting to feel safe. And in a church where some grieve what has been lost and others rejoice in what God is doing now, let both be heard, for his steadfast love endures forever.
3.theology:
The altar comes before the house. For years the returned community worshipped at an altar standing among ruins, and the order is the gospel's: the place where sin is atoned for comes first, and the dwelling of God is built around it.

Verse 11 sings the old refrain of steadfast love over bare foundation stones, with no cloud and no fire, and verses 12-13 hold grief and joy in one sound without rebuking either.
3.examples:
The first thing the returnees built in Jerusalem was an altar in the open air on a hill of rubble, and they built it because they were afraid. They kept the feast's offerings to the last bull, and ordered cedar exactly as Solomon had.

When the foundation was laid, the old men's weeping and the young men's shouting made one noise, and the noise brought the adversaries.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Set the Altar in Its Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The returned exiles put the worship of God before everything else, even before their own safety. In the holy seventh month they gather “as one man” in Jerusalem (v. 1). Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar “as it is written in the Law of Moses” (v. 2), and they set it on its old site, “for fear was on them”, so that the morning and evening offerings rise again (v. 3). They keep the Feast of Booths and restore the whole calendar of sacrifice, with freewill gifts besides (vv. 4–5), though “the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid” (v. 6). Then they pay workmen and send to Tyre and Sidon for cedar, as Solomon had (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is not the reward for finishing the building; it is the first thing, and everything else is built around it. Yet the smoke had to rise every day, because no lamb could finish the work. Hebrews draws the contrast: every priest stands daily offering sacrifices that can never take away sins, but Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins and sat down (Heb 10:11-12).
verseByVerse.examples: A frightened people did not wait until they felt safe to worship. They worshipped because they did not feel safe.

verseByVerse.quote: When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God. They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frightened and surrounded, the returned exiles built the altar first and offered the sacrifices God commanded, because they needed God before they needed walls.

When the seventh month came. The seventh month was the holy month of Israel’s year, with the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths (Leviticus 23). The families have barely unpacked, and they walk back up to Jerusalem “as one man”.

They built the altar of the God of Israel. What they build first tells you everything: not houses, not walls, not the temple, which will not stand for twenty years, but an altar on the ruins, in the open air. Because the work is an altar, the high priest’s name comes first (see Joshua the high priest). And after half a century without one, nobody improvises: “as it is written in the Law of Moses”.

For fear was on them. The fear is not an obstacle they overcame; it is given as the reason. A few thousand families in a ruined city, surrounded by peoples who did not want them there, and so they built the altar.

Morning and evening. The daily sacrifice had stopped when Ahaz shut the temple doors (2 Chronicles 29:7), and stopped again when the house burned. Now, for the first time in two generations, there is smoke over Jerusalem that is not the smoke of a burning city.

A better altar. Every burnt offering on that altar said that sinners could come near to God only through a sacrifice offered in their place. It pointed beyond itself to the cross, where Christ “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12). We have an altar, Hebrews says (Hebrews 13:10), and it is never closed.

What faith does with fear. Faith does not wait to feel safe before it worships; it goes to the one place where the frightened are met by God. Whoever is afraid tonight has the same instruction, and a better altar: do not first fix the fear; go to the God who has already dealt with your sin.
verseByVerse.note: The seventh month (September–October) held the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths. Jeshua the high priest is called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah.

verseByVerse.quote: And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required, and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD. From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid. So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people kept God’s feasts exactly as written and gave beyond what was required, though there was still no temple, only an altar among the ruins.

They kept the Feast of Booths. At the Feast of Booths Israel lived for a week in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness. For these people it hardly needed acting out; most of them were still living in something temporary.

By number according to the rule. The law is precise to the point of strangeness: thirteen bulls on the first day, twelve on the second, one fewer each day down to seven on the seventh, seventy bulls across the week (Numbers 29:13–32). The returned exiles kept the countdown bull by bull. People who have just come back from losing everything through their own unfaithfulness do not treat the details as optional.

The offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering. Then the whole calendar restarted, the regular offerings, the new moons and the appointed feasts, and people gave freewill offerings beyond what it asked.

The foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid. An altar standing by itself on a hill of rubble, smoke rising twice a day, and all around it the burned stones of the house: no walls, no roof, no Holy Place, no ark. Worship had come back before the building did. God is not bound to a building, and his people can worship him wherever they are.

Cedar trees from Lebanon. The order for cedar repeats Solomon’s contract almost clause for clause: payment in food to Tyre, and timber “in rafts by sea to Joppa” (2 Chronicles 2:10, 16). The second house is begun exactly as the first was.

Booths and the Word made flesh. Centuries later, on the last day of this same feast, Jesus stood up in the temple courts and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The feast that remembered God’s care for his people in the wilderness found its fulfilment in the One who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Sound Was Heard Far Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s steadfast love is sung over a smaller house, with tears and shouts together. In the second year the work begins, supervised by the Levites (vv. 8–9). When the foundation is laid, priests with trumpets and the sons of Asaph with cymbals praise the LORD, as David had directed, and sing the old refrain, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel”, while the people shout (vv. 10–11). But the old men who had seen Solomon’s house weep aloud, and the weeping and the shouting are so mixed that no one can tell them apart; the sound carries far away (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The song in verse 11 is the one Israel sang when the glory filled Solomon's house. Here there is only a row of foundation stones in a ruined city, and they sing exactly the same words: God's steadfast love did not depend on the glory being visible.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sounds were right. The old men were not faithless for weeping, and the young were not shallow for shouting. God's people have always lived with both sounds at once, and this is the passage that gives them permission.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD. And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers. And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel. And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the foundation was laid, priests and singers praised God with the old song of his goodness and steadfast love, now sung over a people brought back from exile.

In the second month. Solomon, too, “began to build in the second month” (2 Chronicles 3:2). The writer keeps setting the new house down on the pattern of the old one.

From twenty years old and upward. Not an emergency concession. Moses set the Levites’ service from twenty-five (Numbers 8:24), and David at the end of his life moved it to twenty: “by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward” (1 Chronicles 23:27). With seventy-four Levites in the whole caravan (2:40), they needed every one.

According to the directions of David king of Israel. The sons of Asaph, the singers of 2:41, play the instruments their ancestors played, in the order David had set (see Priests and Levites).

For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever. A reader who has come through Chronicles knows that song. The Levites sang it when the ark came to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34). They sang it at the dedication of Solomon’s house, and as they sang the house was filled with a cloud, “so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God” (2 Chronicles 5:13–14). The people sang it on their faces when fire fell on the altar (7:3), and Jehoshaphat’s choir sang it marching out before his army (20:21).

Toward Israel. Now it is sung over a row of foundation stones. There is no cloud, no fire, and no ark, and there never will be again. And they sing the same words, and add two of their own: “toward Israel”. His steadfast love endures forever toward us, the people who were sent into exile for their sins and have just walked home. It was true in Babylon, where there was no altar at all; it is true on a building site; and it is true on the worst morning of anyone’s life. The people’s “great shout” is the phrase used of Jericho, the day the walls came down (Joshua 6:5).

What steadfast love means. We use the word love for a feeling, and feelings come and go, so a love that lasts forever can sound like poetry. The Hebrew word, hesed, is sturdier: love that has bound itself by a promise, loyal covenant love that keeps going when the other party has given it every reason to stop. Most of us quietly assume that God’s kindness rises and falls with our performance, and so we swing between anxiety and pride. Timothy Keller often pointed out that religion runs on I obey, therefore I am accepted, while the gospel turns it round: I am accepted, therefore I obey. Steadfast love is the root of that turning. It reached its height when God kept his promise at the cost of his own Son: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). So on the morning when you have least to show him, sing the refrain anyway. It was written for people like these. See Steadfast Love in the Theological Dictionary.

When was the foundation laid? Haggai dates the laying of the foundation to 520 BC (Haggai 2:18), but here it is the second year after the return, probably about 536. The likeliest answer is that the foundation was first laid then, and when the work resumed in 520 after sixteen years of neglect, it was laid again or completed.

Uncertain wording. In verse 9 the Hebrew calls Kadmiel and his sons “the sons of Judah”, which is odd for Levites. It is probably another spelling of Hodaviah, the Levite family named alongside Jeshua and Kadmiel in 2:40. The Jeshua of verse 9 is that Levite, not the high priest of verse 8.

verseByVerse.quote: But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy, so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The old men who remembered Solomon’s temple wept over the smaller foundation, while the young shouted for joy, and God let both sounds rise together.

Old men who had seen the first house. Solomon’s temple was burned in 587 or 586, and this foundation is laid about fifty years later. Anyone who remembered it was now nearing sixty at least, and had walked its courts as a child holding a father’s hand. They remembered the size of it, the gold, the bronze pillars, the crowds at the feasts.

When they saw the foundation of this house being laid. Not vague nostalgia but a measurement: the foundation lines were marked out in front of them, and the new house would be smaller. Haggai spoke to exactly these men sixteen years later, and he did not pretend: “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?” (Haggai 2:3). He granted every word of their grief.

Many shouted aloud for joy. The younger people, born in Babylon, had no gold on the walls to measure against, only the promise that God would bring his people back, and here was a foundation to prove it. For them any foundation was a miracle, and they were right too.

The people could not distinguish the sound. Anyone a little way off heard one noise, and could not have told whether Jerusalem was celebrating or grieving. It was doing both, at full volume.

The sound was heard far away. And the sound carried: “Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard” (4:1). Joy in God’s work is audible a long way off, and not everyone who hears it is glad.

The greater glory. Haggai answered the old men’s grief with a promise they could not have understood: “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (Haggai 2:9). It was. Solomon’s temple had the gold and the cloud; it never had the Son of God in it. This one did. Into this house, rebuilt and enlarged but still the second house, a baby was carried to be presented, a twelve-year-old sat among the teachers asking questions, and a grown man drove out the money-changers and called it his Father’s house. The old men mourned a building that was smaller. They had just laid the foundation of the only temple the Lord of the temple ever walked into.

A picture of the church. This is as honest a picture of the church as the Old Testament gives: people who remember better days and grieve what has been lost, and people who see only the grace of what God is doing now and cannot stop shouting about it. A church that only shouts has forgotten what was lost; a church that only weeps has forgotten who laid the foundation. The book does not ask either group to be quiet.

Nostalgia and progress. The two sounds are also the two great moods of modern public life. One looks back: things were better once, and the task is to recover what was lost. The other looks forward: the past was a cage, and the future will be better simply because it is later. Both make the present hard to live in, the first because today is never as good as yesterday, the second because today is never as good as tomorrow. Israel’s hope lay neither in its past nor in progress but in a God who keeps his promises whatever the size of the building. Christians remember, because God has acted in history, and they hope, because he has said he is making all things new (Revelation 21:5). But they live today, which is where his steadfast love is sung.

keyVerse.quote: And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This is the song Israel sang when the glory filled Solomon’s temple, now sung over a bare foundation by a people brought back from exile for their sins. The added words “toward Israel” confess that God’s covenant love had outlasted their unfaithfulness. It is the heart of the chapter: worship rests not on the size of the building but on the steadfastness of God.

3.reflection:
The returned exiles built the altar before anything else, “for fear was on them” (v. 3). What do you tend to do first when you are afraid? What would it look like to go first to God through Christ?

They kept the Feast of Booths “as it is written”, down to the number of bulls each day (v. 4). How can we take God’s word seriously in the details without slipping into thinking our carefulness earns his favour?

They sang that the LORD’s steadfast love endures forever “toward Israel”, the people who had been exiled for their sins (v. 11). How does God’s covenant love differ from love that depends on our performance, and where do you need to believe it this week?

Some wept for the past and some shouted for joy, and the sounds could not be told apart (vv. 12–13). Where do you see these two responses in your church, and how can each learn from the other?

4.title: The Long Delay: Opposition, Discouragement, and Silence
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel,<sup>2</sup>they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here."<sup>3</sup>But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."<sup>4</sup>Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build<sup>5</sup>and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.<sup>6</sup>And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>7</sup>In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated.<sup>8</sup>Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows:<sup>9</sup>Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites,<sup>10</sup>and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River.<sup>11</sup>(This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now<sup>12</sup>be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.<sup>13</sup>Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired.<sup>14</sup>Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king,<sup>15</sup>in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste.<sup>16</sup>We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."<sup>17</sup>The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now<sup>18</sup>the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me.<sup>19</sup>And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it.<sup>20</sup>And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid.<sup>21</sup>Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me.<sup>22</sup>And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?"<sup>23</sup>Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.<sup>24</sup>Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
4.overview:
