Where we are. Chapter 3 ended with a shout “heard far away” as the temple’s foundation was laid. Chapter 4 shows who heard it, and how the work was stopped. Out of time order, it gathers in opposition from the next ninety years.

The message. God’s work always meets opposition, first in the form of a friendly offer to compromise and then in the form of fear, pressure and accusation. The people of God must refuse to mix the worship of the LORD with other gods, even when refusal costs them. Opposition may stop the work for a time, but it cannot stop God: the chapter ends with the work halted “until” a set day, and the next chapter shows that day arriving.

Why it was said. The first readers knew what it was to be small, watched and slandered, and to see good work stall for years (see the introduction). This chapter tells them that this has always been the pattern, and that God sets the limits of every delay.

How the chapter makes its case. The adversaries offer to help build, claiming to worship the same God, and are refused because their worship was mixed with other gods (vv. 1–3). So they discourage and frighten the builders and bribe officials against them until the reign of Darius (vv. 4–5). Then the writer leaps forward: an accusation under Xerxes (v. 6), and under Artaxerxes a letter in Aramaic warning that the Jews are rebuilding the walls of a rebellious city and will stop paying taxes (vv. 7–16). The king searches his records, finds the charge true, and stops the work by force (vv. 17–23). Verse 24 steps back to the temple, halted until the second year of Darius.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by God’s character revealed in Christ. The quarrel with the Samaritans that begins here ran on until Jesus told a Samaritan woman that true worshippers would worship the Father “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23), drawing people from both sides to one worship through himself. The accusers read out a true record; the gospel answers such accusations not by denying the record but by Christ, who died and intercedes for his people (Romans 8:33–34). And the stalled temple points to the greater building Christ promised: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

For us. Not every offer to build together is an offer to build the same thing; the test is whether God alone is wanted. When opposition wears you down, take your fear to God rather than let it drive you from the work. And when the accuser reads out your record, answer him with Christ.
4.theology: The first opposition is an offer of help, and what verse 3 refuses is a partnership with a mixed religion, not people who want to come to God. Verses 6-23 are arranged by theme, not date, so that ninety years of opposition can be seen whole. And the accusation that finally works is a true one; the answer to it, as the end of the chapter shows, is not denial but God's own verdict on his people.
4.examples: The narrator calls them adversaries before they say a single friendly word, and in their own offer they admit that Assyria brought them there. The king's archive, searched to condemn Jerusalem, also confirmed that mighty kings once ruled the whole region from it. Meanwhile the foundation lay in the ground for sixteen years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Let Us Build with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first threat to God’s work comes as a friendly offer, and only when it is refused does it turn hostile. When the adversaries hear of the building, they ask to share it, saying they have worshipped the same God since the Assyrians brought them there (vv. 1–2). Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse, pointing to the commission Cyrus gave them (v. 3), because these people worshipped the LORD alongside other gods. Then the friendliness ends. The people of the land weaken the builders’ hands, frighten them, and hire officials to work against them for the rest of Cyrus’s reign and into the reign of Darius, some sixteen years (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The offer sounded like worship, but the history behind it was the one told in 2 Kings 17. What was refused was a joint building with a mixed religion, not a person who wanted God.
verseByVerse.examples: The most dangerous opposition in this chapter is the first, and it arrives smiling. Nobody threatens anyone in verse 2. They offer to help, and they use the right words to do it. The threats come only after the help has been declined, which tells you what the help was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here." But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When their neighbours offered to help build, the leaders refused, because these people worshipped the LORD as one god among many, and God’s house could not be built as a shrine to mixed worship.

The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin. The last chapter ended with a sound “heard far away” (3:13), and this is who heard it. The writer calls them adversaries before they speak, for nothing they say will sound hostile.

Let us build with you. The offer contains its own history: “who brought us here”. These are the descendants of the peoples Assyria planted in Samaria after it emptied the northern kingdom, “from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim” (2 Kings 17:24). Esarhaddon (about 681–669 BC) seems to have added settlers of his own a generation later, which is why they name him. And the book of Kings describes their religion in one sentence: “they feared the LORD but also served their own gods” (2 Kings 17:33), and their children did the same “to this day” (17:41).

For we worship your God as you do. Half true, and the missing half is the point: they worshipped the LORD as one god among several, and building together would have made his house one shrine among several.

You have nothing to do with us. It sounds hard, but the rest of the book shows what it did not mean: not that no outsider could ever join them. Two chapters later the Passover is eaten by the returned exiles “and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD” (6:21). Anyone could come in who came to the LORD alone. What was refused was a partnership with a religion that kept its other gods, and the ground given is the commission itself: “as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us”. They had no authority to share out the task.

Christ and the Samaritans. The quarrel begun here ran on for centuries, and Jesus walked into the middle of it. To a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well he said plainly that “salvation is from the Jews”, and then opened a door neither side expected: the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:22–23). Christ gathers people from both sides into one worship of the one God, through himself.

The same offer today. Churches meet this offer still, with the right vocabulary. Not every invitation to build together is an invitation to build the same thing. The test is not whether the other party uses the name of God, but whether they want God alone.

What it does not mean. Not a refusal to love or live peaceably with neighbours of other beliefs, nor suspicion of Christians who differ on lesser matters. It concerns the worship of God and the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.note: These adversaries were settlers brought in by Assyria, in part forerunners of the Samaritans.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refused a share in the work, the neighbours set out to stop it by discouragement, fear and bribery, and for sixteen years they succeeded.

The people of the land discouraged the people of Judah. Literally, they “weakened the hands” of the people of Judah: they sapped the strength to work. In the last chapter fear drove them to the altar (3:3); now it drives them off the building site. The same emotion has opposite results, depending on where it is taken.

Bribed counselors against them. Not a mob with torches but a funded, patient campaign at court. It worked: the foundation laid with such noise sat in the ground for some sixteen years.

How good work is usually stopped. Most good work of God is stopped not by catastrophe but by steady pressure, until those who began it with shouting quietly go back to their own affairs. Haggai will arrive to tell them exactly that: they were living in their “paneled houses” while the house of God lay in ruins (Haggai 1:4). Christ promises that the gates of hell will not prevail against his church (Matthew 16:18); he does not promise it will never be slowed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–24 — Be It Known to the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Opposition to God’s people was not a single incident but a pattern, and the writer gathers it together to show it. He leaps forward to an accusation under Xerxes (v. 6) and a letter under Artaxerxes, quoted in the Aramaic in which it was sent, warning the king that the Jews are rebuilding the walls of a rebellious city that will stop paying tribute (vv. 7–16). The king searches his archives, finds the charge true, and orders the work stopped until he decrees otherwise; his officials stop it by force (vv. 17–23). Then verse 24 returns to the temple: work on the house of God ceased until the second year of Darius.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 6-23 leap forward in time to letters about the city wall, and verse 24 steps back to the temple in Darius's day. For orientation, the Persian kings behind these chapters, with approximate dates, are Cyrus (took Babylon in 539, died 530), Cambyses (530-522, not named in Ezra), Darius I (522-486), Xerxes, the Ahasuerus of Esther (486-465), and his son Artaxerxes I (465-424).
verseByVerse.examples: The accusers did not need to lie. They took Judah's real past and used it to forbid Judah's future.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer now leaps forward decades to show that opposition to God’s people was a pattern, not an incident: whenever they built in Jerusalem, someone wrote to the king.

A jump in time. Ahasuerus (v. 6) is Xerxes, the king of the book of Esther, who came to the throne about thirty years after the temple was finished. Artaxerxes (v. 7) was his son, later still. And what the Artaxerxes letter complains about is not the temple but the city: “They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations” (v. 12).

A pattern, not an incident. The writer is not confused about the Persian kings. He gathers opposition from ninety years into one chapter: whenever God’s people built anything in Jerusalem, somebody wrote to the king. Verse 24 will step back to the temple and pick up the thread from verse 5.

Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel. Nothing more is known of them. Mithredath is a Persian name and Tabeel an Aramaic one meaning “God is good”: a mixed group of local officials. Their letter is not quoted; the next one (v. 8) may be the same complaint sent on, or a second letter.

The letter was written in Aramaic. From 4:8 to 6:18 the book itself is written in Aramaic, the language of Persian government, so the letters are given in the language they were sent in (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in verse 7 are unclear. “Bishlam” may be a man’s name, or the Hebrew may be a phrase meaning “in peace” or “with the approval of”, describing how the letter was sent. And “written in Aramaic and translated” is compressed: it may mean the letter was written in Aramaic script and the Aramaic language, or that it was written in Aramaic and then translated for the king.
verseByVerse.note: From 4:8 to 6:18 the book is written in Aramaic (ESV note), the language of Persian government.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows: Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites, and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers opened their letter by presenting themselves as a whole loyal province, set against a handful of troublesome Jews.

Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe. The letter opens by listing everyone who signed it: judges, governors, officials, Persians, men of Erech and Babylon and Susa, and all “the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported”. The king is meant to see a whole loyal province against a few Jews.

The nations whom … Osnappar deported. When Assyria took Samaria it moved conquered peoples into the land in place of the exiled northern tribes (2 Kings 17:24), and later kings added more. These are the same settlers who had offered to help build the temple, claiming to have sacrificed to the LORD since the days of Esarhaddon (see the note on vv. 1–3). Refused a share in the work, their descendants now sign a letter to stop it.

Uncertain wording. Osnappar is not named anywhere else. He is probably Ashurbanipal, the last great king of Assyria (about 668–627 BC), but this cannot be proved. Some of the titles in verse 9 are also uncertain; the ESV’s “judges, the governors, the officials” translate Persian words whose exact meaning is debated, and some take them as the names of peoples instead.

verseByVerse.quote: (This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations. Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter accuses Jerusalem of a history of rebellion and warns the king that a rebuilt city will stop paying his taxes.

That rebellious and wicked city. The charge of rebellion was true. Jerusalem had rebelled: its last king broke an oath sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chronicles 36:13), and the city was burned for it.

The Jews who came up from you to us. This probably refers to a later party of returning exiles, perhaps those who came with Ezra in Artaxerxes’ seventh year (7:7), who had begun to repair the city walls.

They will not pay tribute, custom, or toll. Then the letter turns to what a king cares about most, his revenue. The fear was not foolish: Egypt rebelled early in Artaxerxes’ reign, about 460 BC, and a walled city on the road there could look like the start of another revolt.

Uncertain wording. The three tax words in verse 13 are borrowed administrative terms of uncertain exact meaning, probably the regular provincial tribute, a tax paid in goods, and a levy on land or on travel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king, in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste. We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers posed as loyal servants and urged the king to check his own records, sure that Jerusalem’s past would condemn it.

Because we eat the salt of the palace. An idiom for being in the king’s pay and bound to him by it, so that informing on Jerusalem looks like simple loyalty.

In order that search may be made. They invite the king to check his own archives, confident of what he will find (v. 19). Their last line is a gross exaggeration: one small walled city could hardly cost the king the whole province. Fear works by making the threat bigger than it is.

How the accuser works. Satan, the accuser, works the same way. He rarely needs to lie about a believer’s history. He only needs to read it out at the moment the believer is trying to build something for God, and suggest that people with a record like that should not be allowed to start again. The answer is not to deny the record but to point to Christ (see the note on v. 24).

verseByVerse.quote: The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me. And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it. And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid. Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me. And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?" Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king searched the records, found the charge true, and stopped the rebuilding of the city, but he left open the possibility of a later decree.

Mighty kings have been over Jerusalem. The reply contains a sentence the accusers can hardly have wanted: the Persian archives remember David and Solomon, and this ruined little town once governed the whole region beyond the Euphrates. The search meant to condemn Jerusalem turned up evidence of its glory as well.

Until a decree is made by me. The king left a door open without meaning to. Years later the same Artaxerxes would look at his cupbearer’s sad face and give Nehemiah letters to rebuild these very walls (Nehemiah 2:1–8). The decree that stopped the work contained the words that would one day restart it. God holds the hearts of kings as surely when they say “stop” as when they say “build” (Proverbs 21:1).

By force and power made them cease. The order was enforced in haste and by force. That broken wall is probably the one Nehemiah heard about in Susa, which made him sit down and weep (Nehemiah 1:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple work stood still for some sixteen years, but only until the day God had set for it to begin again.

The work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped. The writer steps back to the story he left at verse 5. Nothing more was built on the house until Darius’s second year, 520 BC, about sixteen years after the foundation was laid.

Sixteen idle years. A child born the week the foundation was laid was a teenager before another stone went up, while the altar still smoked and weeds grew in the trench. This is one of the most honest verses in the Old Testament for anyone who has given years to a work of God that stalled: it records sixteen years of nothing, and does not hurry past them.

Until the second year of the reign of Darius. But it records them with an end date. The stoppage was real but not permanent, and the God who let it happen had already decided when it would end.

The accusation answered. The accusation of verse 15 was answered not by proving it false but by God himself. Zechariah, who appears in the next chapter, saw Jeshua the high priest, who built the altar in chapter 3, standing before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes, “and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him”. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. And the LORD said, “The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! … Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?”, and ordered the filthy garments taken off and clean ones put on (Zechariah 3:1–5).

The record taken away. That is still how the charge sheet is dealt with: by the One who has taken the record away. “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died … who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:33–34).
verseByVerse.note: Darius I reigned 522–486 BC; work resumed in his second year, 520 BC.

keyVerse.quote: Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s long story of opposition ends here, and the verse is honest: the enemies succeeded and the work stood still for years. Yet the word “until” carries the hope of the whole book. The delay had an end date set by God, and the next chapter shows his word getting the work moving again.

4.reflection:
The adversaries offered to help, saying “we worship your God as you do” (v. 2), but their worship was mixed with other gods. How can a church tell the difference between true partnership in the gospel and an offer that would compromise it? Why does the refusal not mean shutting the door on outsiders (6:21)?

The opposition worked by weakening hands, spreading fear and wearing people down over years (vv. 4–5). Where do you see that kind of slow pressure today, in your own life or your church? What helps God’s people keep going?

The accusers did not need to lie; they read out Jerusalem’s true record (vv. 15, 19). How does the accuser use our past against us, and how does the gospel answer him (Zechariah 3:1–5; Romans 8:33–34)?

The work stopped for some sixteen years, but only “until” the time God had set (v. 24). How does it help to know that God sets the limits of every delay? What work of God are you tempted to give up on?

5.title: The Prophets Arise: Haggai, Zechariah, and the Resumption of Work
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them.<sup>2</sup>Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.<sup>3</sup>At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?"<sup>4</sup>They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?"<sup>5</sup>But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.<sup>6</sup>This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king.<sup>7</sup>They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace.<sup>8</sup>Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands.<sup>9</sup>Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?'<sup>10</sup>We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.<sup>11</sup>And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.<sup>12</sup>But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia.<sup>13</sup>However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt.<sup>14</sup>And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor;<sup>15</sup>and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site."<sup>16</sup>Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.'<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 ended with the work on the temple stopped by force and the site left idle until the second year of Darius, 520 BC (4:24). Some sixteen years have passed since the foundation was laid, and nothing in the political situation has changed.

The message. God restarts his stalled work by his word, and he watches over those who obey it. Two prophets preach, the leaders rise and build, and when the Persian governor comes asking questions, “the eye of their God was on the elders” (v. 5). The builders do not know how the inquiry will end, but they tell the truth, including the truth about their fathers’ sin, and keep working while the king decides.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small community living under Persian officials, who could stop them with a letter (see the introduction). This chapter shows them that obedience does not wait for every official question to be settled, and that God rules the outcome of inquiries they cannot control.

How the chapter makes its case. Haggai and Zechariah prophesy, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to build with the prophets beside them (vv. 1–2). Tattenai the governor asks who authorised the work and who the builders are, but God’s eye is on the elders, and the work goes on while the report goes to Darius (vv. 3–5). Tattenai’s letter is fair: a great house of huge stones, a work that “prospers in their hands” (vv. 6–10). It records the elders’ answer: they are servants of the God of heaven and earth, the first house fell because their fathers angered God, and Cyrus decreed the rebuilding and returned the vessels (vv. 11–16). So let the archives be searched (v. 17).

Where it leads. By promise. The two men the prophets stirred carried Israel’s two great offices, king and priest. Haggai called Zerubbabel, David’s heir, God’s “signet ring” (Haggai 2:23), and Zechariah crowned Jeshua as a sign of “the man whose name is the Branch”, who “shall build the temple of the LORD” and be “a priest on his throne” (Zechariah 6:12–13). Neither man was that Branch. Jesus is: the King-Priest who builds a temple of his own body and of his people (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:21–22), and who sent his church out to build with the same promise Haggai gave, “I am with you” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. Stalled faith is restarted by God’s word heard and obeyed, not by waiting for circumstances to change. When you face questions you cannot control, keep doing what God has told you, for his eye is on you. And because Christ has borne your sin, you can name your past honestly, without fear.
5.theology:
The work of God restarts when the word of God is preached: nothing in the political situation changed between chapter 4 and chapter 5, but two prophets spoke. Verse 5 says that God was watching, without saying how the inquiry would end, and verse 12 shows the only safe way to hold a guilty past, which is to confess it plainly. The accusers of chapter 4 had used Jerusalem's history as a weapon; here the builders name their fathers' sin themselves.

The two leaders the prophets stirred carried the two offices Israel's hope rested on, and the prophets pointed beyond both men to someone greater. Haggai called Zerubbabel, the heir of David, God's signet ring (Hag 2:23), and Zerubbabel stands in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:12-13). Zechariah crowned Jeshua the priest as a sign of the man whose name is the Branch, who shall build the temple of the LORD and be a priest on his throne (Zech 6:11-13). The house they built was real stone. The King-Priest it pointed to builds a temple of his own body and of his people (John 2:19-21; Eph 2:21-22).
5.examples: The prophets did not preach and leave; they were on the building site, supporting the men they had rebuked. And the governor who came to investigate reported that the work was going on diligently and prospering, while the builders kept at it for the weeks it took his letter to reach the king and come back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Eye of Their God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Preaching restarts the work, and God’s eye keeps it going. After sixteen years of nothing, two prophets speak “in the name of the God of Israel who was over them” (v. 1), and Zerubbabel and Jeshua rise and begin to rebuild, with the prophets beside them on the site (v. 2). Almost at once Tattenai, the governor of the whole province west of the Euphrates, arrives asking who authorised the building and who the builders are (vv. 3–4). The reader of chapter 4 expects the work to stop again. Instead, “the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews” (v. 5), and the building goes on while the question travels to Darius and back.
verseByVerse.theology: Sixteen years of nothing end in two verses, and what ends them is preaching. Haggai dated his first sermon to the first day of the sixth month (Hag 1:1), and on the twenty-fourth of the same month the people were back on the site.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the chapter's comfort: the builders did not know how the inquiry would end, and they kept working while it was pending.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After sixteen years of silence God spoke through two prophets, and the leaders rose and began to build, with the prophets working beside them.

Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah. Nothing else had changed: the officials and the bare foundation were all still there. What changed was that God spoke, through Haggai and then Zechariah in 520 BC (Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 1:1), in the name of the God “who was over them”, above Persia.

Haggai’s sermons. They are not gentle. “Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4). The people said the time had not yet come (Haggai 1:2); Haggai pointed out that it had come soon enough for their own carpentry, and told them, “Consider your ways” (Haggai 1:5).

I am with you. The rebuke was followed by a promise, not a threat: “I am with you, declares the LORD” (Haggai 1:13). Then, in this book’s own verb, “the LORD stirred up the spirit” of Zerubbabel, of Joshua and of all the remnant, and “they came and worked on the house” (Haggai 1:14). The God who stirred Cyrus and the families who went home (1:1, 5) stirs his people again, this time by a sermon, and twenty-three days after the first sermon the work began (Haggai 1:15).

The prophets of God were with them, supporting them. The preachers did not go home after preaching. They were on the site, beside the men they had rebuked. Zechariah named where the strength came from: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6).

The builder they pointed to. Zerubbabel, David’s heir, and Jeshua, the high priest, were signs of a greater builder: Zechariah crowned Jeshua as a sign of “the man whose name is the Branch”, who “shall build the temple of the LORD” (Zechariah 6:12). Jesus, Zerubbabel’s descendant (Matthew 1:12–13), is that builder, and his temple is his people (Ephesians 2:21–22).

How God restarts stalled work. That is still how God restarts stalled work: by a word plainly spoken, and by his Spirit, who now lives in his people and gives them strength to obey it. A drifting Christian does not first need better circumstances, but to hear God and obey, with others beside him.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?" They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?" But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the governor came asking who had authorised the building, God was watching over the builders, and they kept working while the matter went to the king.

Who gave you a decree to build this house? After chapter 4 the reader braces for another round of accusation, and the questions sound like it: who authorised this, and what are the builders’ names? Writing down names is what officials do before arrests.

A fair question. Tattenai governs for the Persian crown, and a large building going up in a city with a history of revolt is exactly what he is paid to ask about. “Beyond the River” was the Persian province west of the Euphrates: Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria and Judah together. A Babylonian tablet from Darius’s reign seems to name him as governor. He is a real civil servant doing a real job.

But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews. They did not know how the inquiry would come out; the last time letters went to a Persian king about Jerusalem, the work was stopped by force (4:23). But the one watching them was not Tattenai. “Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him” (Psalm 33:18), and his eyes “run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him” (2 Chronicles 16:9). Here that support was a governor who chose not to stop the work, and builders who kept at it while the letter travelled.

Waiting on a decision. Anyone waiting on a decision they cannot control, a hearing, a medical result, a letter that could go either way, can take this verse personally, for the Father who numbers the hairs of our heads (Matthew 10:30) is watching still. The outcome was not yet known. The eye was already on them. They went on working.

Textual note. In verse 4 the Aramaic text reads, literally, then we said to them, as if the writer were speaking as one of the builders; some early translations read “they asked them”, which the ESV follows. Either way, the officials wanted the builders’ names.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — We Are the Servants of the God of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tattenai’s report to Darius is fair, and the elders’ answer inside it is honest to the point of confession. The governor describes a great house of huge stones and a work that “prospers in their hands” (vv. 6–10). Then he records what the elders told him: they are servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding a house a great king of Israel once built (v. 11); it was destroyed because their fathers angered God (v. 12); Cyrus decreed its rebuilding and sent back the vessels with Sheshbazzar, and the work has been under way ever since (vv. 13–16). The letter ends by asking the king to search the archives (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Asked by a Persian official why their temple had been destroyed, the elders did not blame Babylon. They named the real offence themselves.
verseByVerse.examples: Tattenai is not the villain the reader expects after chapter 4. He asks the right question, lets the work continue while he asks it, describes the building accurately and even admiringly, and asks the king to check the builders' claim rather than his own suspicions. An honest official is a gift of God, and the text takes the trouble to show us one.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king. They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace. Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands. Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?' We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The governor’s report to Darius was fair: he described a great house well built and a work going on diligently, and took the names for the king’s information, not as a charge.

This is a copy of the letter. The surprise is how fair it is. The letter of chapter 4 called Jerusalem “that rebellious and wicked city” (4:12) and went for the king’s revenue. This one calls the building “the house of the great God” and reports that “this work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands”. Even the names are taken “for your information”: a file, not a charge.

Built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. Solid work, built as Cyrus’s decree had specified, with courses of stone and timber (6:4).

Honest questions. Not every questioner is an enemy, though after long opposition a person can hear every enquiry as an attack. Tattenai asked hard questions honestly and wrote down the answers straight, and God used his fairness as surely as the prophets’ sermons.

Uncertain wording. The Aramaic for “huge stones” means literally stones of rolling. Most take it to mean blocks too large to carry, which had to be rolled into place; some think it means dressed or polished stone. Either way it describes solid, costly work.

verseByVerse.quote: And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished. But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia. However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt. And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor; and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site." Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.' Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders answered as servants of the God of heaven, confessing that their fathers’ sin had brought the destruction, appealing to Cyrus’s decree and inviting the king to check it.

We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth. The first thing they say about themselves is “servants”: not of Persia, but of the God who made heaven and earth, a large claim to make to a governor, and made before they mention anybody’s decree.

Because our fathers had angered the God of heaven. The charge of rebellion in chapter 4 worked because it was true; here the builders go further than their accusers: not bad luck, but our fathers angered God, and he handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chronicles 36:15–17).

In the first year of Cyrus. Then they appeal to what Cyrus decreed (1:2–4, 7–11). “From that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished” is a kindly way of describing sixteen years of weeds; Haggai had put it differently (Haggai 1:2). The elders did not lie, since the building had been begun and never officially abandoned, but they chose their words with care.

Let search be made in the royal archives. And they invite the check. In chapter 4 the archive was a weapon against them (4:15); here it is asked for by people with nothing to hide.

Holding a guilty past. Naming their fathers’ sin aloud, to a stranger, is the only safe way to hold a guilty past: people who tell the truth about their own sin cannot be blackmailed with it. The accuser’s leverage is always the thing we are hiding, and they had stopped hiding it.

Building on a promise. They built on, not knowing what the search would find, resting on a decree they could not produce and Haggai’s one-line promise, “I am with you, declares the LORD.” It is the promise the Lord Jesus gave to the church when he sent it out to build something far larger than a temple, with no decree to show the world’s governors except his word: “And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

The tiring work of keeping up appearances. Much modern anxiety comes from managing a reputation: we curate what others see and live with a low hum of fear that someone will find the photograph, the old message, the thing we said. The elders had a past, and they named it first. That freedom comes not from a thicker skin but from having been judged and pardoned: whoever knows God’s verdict on his sin fell on Christ has nothing left to protect from anyone else’s. Paul could call himself the foremost of sinners in a letter to be read in churches (1 Timothy 1:15), because his standing did not rest on his record. The gospel does not polish our past. It frees us from having to.

Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel? Verse 16 says Sheshbazzar laid the foundations, but chapter 3 names Zerubbabel. Either Sheshbazzar was the governor under whose authority it was laid (1:8), or the two names belong to one man.

keyVerse.quote: But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the chapter. The governor’s questions sound like the start of another shutdown, but the writer looks past Tattenai to the God who was watching, and the work goes on. It does not say how the inquiry will end; it says who is watching while it is pending, which is the comfort of every believer waiting on a decision they cannot control.

5.reflection:
Nothing changed in Judah between chapters 4 and 5 except that two prophets preached (vv. 1–2). Where has your obedience stalled, and what has God already said about it that you need to act on?

The prophets stayed on the building site “supporting” the men they had rebuked (v. 2). What would it look like for us to stand beside those we challenge, rather than speak and walk away?

The builders kept working while their future was being decided by someone else, because “the eye of their God” was on them (v. 5). What decision are you waiting on, and how does this verse shape the way you wait?

The elders told a stranger plainly that their fathers had angered God (v. 12). Why does the gospel free us to be honest about our past, and where are you still managing appearances?

6.title: The Temple Completed: Darius's Decree, Dedication, and Passover

6.overview:
Where we are. Tattenai’s letter has gone to Darius asking him to search the archives for Cyrus’s decree (5:17). The builders have kept working while they wait, not knowing what the search will find. This chapter brings the answer, the finished house and the first half of the book to its close.

The message. God turns everything round for the good of his people and his house. The archive the accusers used against Jerusalem now produces the decree in its favour; the royal revenue they feared to lose now pays for the building; and a Persian emperor asks the Jews to pray for him. The house is finished, as God had promised through his prophets, and a people brought home keep the Passover with joy, “for the LORD had made them joyful” (v. 22).

Why it was said. The first readers lived with a small temple under foreign kings and could easily think that their history was decided in Persian palaces (see the introduction). This chapter shows them that God rules the kings, and that the house they worshipped in stood by his decree first of all.

How the chapter makes its case. Cyrus’s memorandum is found, not in Babylon but in Ecbatana: rebuild the house at royal cost and return the vessels (vv. 1–5). Darius tells Tattenai to keep away, to pay the builders from the province’s tribute and supply the daily sacrifices, and he guards the edict with a penalty and a blessing (vv. 6–12). The officials obey, and the elders finish the house through the prophets’ preaching in Darius’s sixth year (vv. 13–15). It is dedicated with joy and a sin offering for all twelve tribes (vv. 16–18), and the Passover is kept with every priest clean and room at the table for any who had turned from their gods to the LORD (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The finished house was where God dwelt among his people and sin was atoned for, and Haggai promised that its latter glory would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9); it was, when the Son of God walked into it, and he called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21). The chapter ends with a lamb eaten by exiles brought home and by strangers who had left their gods, and Paul names the fulfilment: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

For us. No opposition can finally stop what God has decreed, so keep doing his work and pray for those who rule over you. Do not try to manufacture joy: look at Christ, the Lamb who brings exiles home and welcomes strangers to his table, and joy will come with the looking.
6.theology:
The chapter is a sequence of reversals, all of them God's. The archive the accusers invoked to prove Jerusalem guilty produces the decree that authorises it, the tribute they feared losing pays for the house, and the empire that rules the lands where the exile began funds the altar.

And the writer credits the finished building not to Darius's money but to the prophets' preaching (v. 14), while the Passover that follows shows what the refusal of chapter 4 meant: it refused a partnership with other gods, never a person who turned to the LORD (v. 21).
6.examples: They searched Babylon for the decree and found it three hundred miles away in a summer palace, and a Persian emperor ended up asking the Jews to pray for his life and his sons. The returnees dedicated their house with a hundred bulls where Solomon had offered 22,000 oxen, and made no apology; and this time every priest and Levite was clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns the weapons of the opposition into help for his house. The search for Cyrus’s decree fails in Babylon, where Tattenai expected it, but a scroll turns up in Ecbatana, the summer capital: Cyrus had ordered the house rebuilt at royal cost and the vessels returned (vv. 1–5). Darius goes far beyond confirming it. He tells Tattenai to keep away, orders the building costs paid from the province’s own tribute, and supplies the daily sacrifices so that the priests may pray for the king and his sons (vv. 6–10). He protects the edict with a savage penalty and calls on the God who made his name dwell in Jerusalem to overthrow anyone who touches it (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The search the accusers asked for turns up the very document that authorises the house, and Darius adds his own decree on top of Cyrus's.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 has a Persian emperor praying in the language of Deuteronomy: the God who has caused his name to dwell there is Moses' phrase for the place God would choose (Deut 12:11). Somebody in that chancery had heard it from the Jews, and the king signed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored. And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found on which this was written: "A record. In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king issued a decree: Concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits, with three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury. And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that is in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. You shall put them in the house of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The search for Cyrus’s decree found it, not where expected but in a distant palace, and the file copy ordered the house rebuilt at the king’s expense and the vessels returned to their places.

In Ecbatana, the citadel. Tattenai had asked the king to look in Babylon (5:17), but it turned up some three hundred miles away in Ecbatana, the old Median capital, where the Persian kings spent their summers. That is how providence often works: not by a voice from heaven but by a clerk who kept the archive properly, and a search that went on after the obvious place came up empty.

A record. What they found was not the proclamation of chapter 1 but the file copy. The public announcement had spoken of the God of heaven and invited volunteers (1:2–4). The office memorandum adds what a treasury wants to know: the place “where sacrifices were offered”, the dimensions, “three layers of great stones and one layer of timber”, and the line that mattered most in Darius’s court: “Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury.”

Each to its place. Then the vessels again, to be restored “each to its place”. Cyrus’s clerks had not only counted them out (1:9–11); they had put in writing that every basin was to go back where it came from. Nothing that belonged to God’s house had been forgotten in Babylon.

Uncertain wording. “Let its foundations be retained” is obscure in Aramaic: it may mean keeping the old foundations or laying new ones firmly. The dimensions also puzzle: no length is given, and sixty cubits wide is three times Solomon’s house (1 Kings 6:2). They may be an upper limit for the royal grant rather than a plan. What is clear is that the king authorised a real house for sacrifice, at his own cost.
verseByVerse.note: Ecbatana was a summer residence of the Persian kings. A copy of Cyrus’s decree was found there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the governors who are in the province Beyond the River, keep away. Let the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site. Moreover, I make a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the rebuilding of this house of God. The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River. And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require—let that be given to them day by day without fail, that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. Also I make a decree that if anyone alters this edict, a beam shall be pulled out of his house, and he shall be impaled on it, and his house shall be made a dunghill. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God that is in Jerusalem. I Darius make a decree; let it be done with all diligence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darius not only confirmed Cyrus’s decree but ordered the governor to stand back, to pay the builders from the province’s taxes and to supply the daily sacrifices, and he protected the house with a curse on anyone who touched it.

Keep away. Darius goes far beyond what anyone had asked. The governor is told to stand back, and Darius adds his own decree on top of Cyrus’s: “The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River.”

The accusers’ fear reversed. Turn back to the letter of chapter 4: if this city is rebuilt, “they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired” (4:13). The revenue the accusers were so anxious to protect is now paid out, by royal order, to build the very thing they were trying to stop. And not only the building: the empire now supplies the altar’s daily ration of animals, wheat, salt, wine and oil, “day by day without fail”.

Pray for the life of the king and his sons. The reason: “that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.” A Persian emperor wants the prayers of the Jews. It is what Jeremiah told the first exiles to do in Babylon: “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). Paul tells the church the same about “kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:1–2). God’s people have always been asked to pray for rulers who did not share their faith; here a ruler asked for it himself.

A Persian penalty. The penalty clause is savage: anyone who alters the edict is to be impaled on a beam pulled from his own house, and his house made a dunghill. That penalty is Darius’s, not God’s. Persian kings did such things, and the text records it without comment.

May the God who has caused his name to dwell there. But the closing blessing is remarkable. “The place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there” is Deuteronomy’s phrase for the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 12:11), and here it is in the mouth of a Persian king. Someone in the chancery had learned it from the Jews, and the emperor put his seal to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — The LORD Had Made Them Joyful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house is finished, and God gives his people joy. Tattenai obeys promptly, and the elders build and prosper through the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, finishing in the sixth year of Darius by the decree of God and of the kings (vv. 13–15). They dedicate the house with joy, offering far less than Solomon did but a sin offering for all twelve tribes, and set the priests and Levites in their divisions as Moses wrote (vv. 16–18). Then, on the right date and with every priest clean, they keep the Passover, sharing it with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the nations to seek the LORD, and they feast with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The house is finished, dedicated and put to use, and at each step the writer notes what God's word had prescribed or promised.
verseByVerse.examples: A small community, drawn almost entirely from two tribes, made its sin offering for all twelve. It would not let Israel shrink to its own size.

verseByVerse.quote: Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia; and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials obeyed, and the elders finished the house through the prophets’ preaching, in the sixth year of Darius, by the decree of God first and of the kings after him.

Did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. The fair official of chapter 5 does his duty promptly.

Through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah. After two imperial decrees and a treasury order, the writer names what the building actually rose on: two preachers. The money came from Darius and the stones from the quarries, but the house was built through the word of God, as Zechariah had promised: “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it” (Zechariah 4:9).

By decree of the God of Israel. God’s decree is first, and the three kings follow it. Cyrus and Darius are obvious; Artaxerxes came to the throne some fifty years after this house was finished, and his name is added because in the next chapter he will send gold and silver “to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem” (7:27). The writer lists every king who served the house, whenever they came.

In the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king. The third of Adar in Darius’s sixth year probably fell in March 515 BC. Solomon’s house was burned in 587 or 586, so some seventy years passed from the fire to the finished house. Jeremiah spoke of seventy years of Babylon’s rule (Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10), and Zechariah, preaching on this building site, asked how long God would be angry “these seventy years” (Zechariah 1:12). Scripture counts the seventy years from more than one starting point, but either way what God had promised came when he said it would. From the first stone to the last, counting the idle years, it had taken about twenty-one years; from Haggai’s first sermon, four and a half.

A greater temple. This is the house Jesus knew, enlarged by Herod but still the second temple, and there he spoke “about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). God truly met his people in the house finished in 515, but it was waiting for the one in whom God would dwell among us in person.
verseByVerse.note: The temple was finished in 515 BC, about seventy years after its destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy. They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The returned exiles dedicated the house with joy, offering what a small community could, yet making atonement for all twelve tribes of Israel, and they set the priests to serve as Moses had written.

Celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy. Many of the old men who wept over the foundation (3:12) were surely dead; their grandchildren stood in the finished courts, and nobody is recorded as weeping.

100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs. At the dedication of Solomon’s house the king offered “22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep” (2 Chronicles 7:5). The returnees did not pretend to be Solomon. They offered what a small, poor community could, and the writer records it without apology.

According to the number of the tribes of Israel. But look at the twelve goats. The community that came home was drawn almost entirely from Judah and Benjamin, and it offered a sin offering for every tribe of Israel, one goat each. Hezekiah’s great sin offering had been seven goats (2 Chronicles 29:21). Though a remnant of a remnant, they would not let Israel shrink to their own size, but made atonement for the whole people, including the tribes scattered by Assyria two centuries earlier.

Atonement for the whole people. “It is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). The twelve goats pointed to the one who shed “his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12), and who gathers into one people the scattered tribes and the nations too.

They set the priests in their divisions. The priests and Levites are set in their divisions “as it is written in the Book of Moses” (see Priests and Levites). With this verse the Aramaic section of the book ends; at verse 19 the story returns to Hebrew, at the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover. For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. So they slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves. It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel. And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The returned exiles kept the Passover on the right day with every priest clean, shared it with all who had turned from their gods to the LORD, and feasted with a joy God himself had given.

On the fourteenth day of the first month. The Passover is kept on the right date. Hezekiah had had to move his Passover to the second month, because “the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number” (2 Chronicles 30:3), and that at the feast many were unclean and the Levites had to kill the lambs for them.

All of them were clean. This time not one priest was unready and not one Levite short: at the first Passover in the rebuilt house, all had made themselves clean in good time.

Every one who had joined them. Verse 21 tells us how to read the refusal of chapter 4. The door was never shut to people. Anyone from the peoples of the land who turned from their gods to the LORD could sit down to this meal, as the law had provided for the stranger at the first Passover (Exodus 12:48). What was refused in chapter 4 was a partnership with other gods; what is welcomed here is a person who has left them.

The LORD had made them joyful. Their joy is God’s gift, like everything else in this book: the spirits stirred in chapter 1, the sermons of chapter 5, the scroll in Ecbatana. They kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, because God had turned a king’s heart. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1).

The heart of the king of Assyria. Darius is called “the king of Assyria”. Assyria had fallen long before, but Persia now ruled its lands, and the old title names the kingdom whose armies began Israel’s exile by carrying the northern tribes away. The power that started the scattering is now paying for the altar.

Christ, our Passover lamb. The first half of Ezra ends with a lamb killed and eaten by a people who had come home, and with foreigners who had turned to God at the same table. It is the right place for it to end. “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the table he keeps is like this one: exiles brought home, strangers who have left their gods (Ephesians 2:19), and a joy that none of them produced for themselves.

Joy cannot be manufactured. Our age has courses, apps and whole shelves of books on how to be happy, and few generations have seemed less sure they had found it. Part of the trouble is that joy does not come to those who aim at it directly. C. S. Lewis made the point in Mere Christianity: “Aim at Heaven and you will get earth ‘thrown in’: aim at earth and you will get neither.” These people did not keep a feast in order to feel joyful. They kept a Passover, remembering a rescue and sharing a lamb with strangers who had turned to God, and the joy was given to them. Joy is what happens when the heart is looking at something better than itself. That is why the gospel produces it where self-improvement cannot: it does not tell us to find joy, but shows us the Lamb, and joy comes with the looking.

keyVerse.quote: And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
keyVerse.note: The first half of the book ends here, and this verse says who did it all. The joy, the finished house and the king’s help were the LORD’s doing, not the people’s achievement. It is the theme of the whole chapter, in which every weapon turned against Jerusalem has been turned round by God for its good.

6.reflection:
The decree turned up in Ecbatana after the search in Babylon came up empty (vv. 1–2). Where have you seen God work through ordinary, unremarkable means? How does that encourage you to keep looking and waiting?

Darius asked the Jews to pray for him and his sons (v. 10). Who are the rulers and authorities you find it hardest to pray for, and what would it look like to pray for their good this week?

The small community offered a sin offering for all twelve tribes, refusing to let Israel shrink to their own size (v. 17). How might our church think too small about God’s people, and how does Christ’s sacrifice enlarge our view?

The Passover table was open to anyone who had separated himself from other gods to seek the LORD (v. 21), and “the LORD had made them joyful” (v. 22). How does the gospel make our churches both holy and welcoming, and where does your joy really come from?

7.title: The Scribe-Priest Arrives: Ezra, the Law, and the Hand of God
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah,<sup>2</sup>son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub,<sup>3</sup>son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth,<sup>4</sup>son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki,<sup>5</sup>son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—<sup>6</sup>this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him.<sup>7</sup>And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.<sup>8</sup>And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king.<sup>9</sup>For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him.<sup>10</sup>For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.<sup>11</sup>This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel:<sup>12</sup>"Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now<sup>13</sup>I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you.<sup>14</sup>For you are sent of you, let it be done with all diligence,<sup>22</sup>up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.<sup>23</sup>Whatever And those who do not know them, you shall teach.<sup>26</sup>Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."<sup>27</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem,<sup>28</sup>and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
7.overview:
Where we are. The temple has stood for nearly sixty years. “Now after this” (v. 1) passes over the whole story of Esther to 458 BC, and the second half of the book begins: the house of God has been rebuilt, and now the people of God are to be rebuilt by the word of God.

The message. God sends his people a teacher of his word, and his hand is on the one who gives himself to that word. Ezra had “set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (v. 10), and God moved the most powerful king on earth to send him with everything he needed. The house is standing; now the people need to know and live by God’s law.

Why it was said. The community in Judah had its temple but was drifting, as chapters 9 and 10 will show (see the introduction). This chapter tells the readers that God’s answer to drift is his word, taught by people who first study and obey it, and that the kings of the earth serve that purpose.

How the chapter makes its case. Ezra, priest of Aaron’s line and scribe skilled in the law, has the hand of the LORD on him (vv. 1–6); he travels with a second company of returning exiles, a four-month journey under God’s good hand, because he had set his heart on the law (vv. 7–10). Artaxerxes’ letter sends him to examine Judah by the law in his hand, funds the altar, frees the temple staff from tax, and commissions him to appoint judges and teach God’s laws (vv. 11–26). Ezra answers with a blessing: God put this into the king’s heart and showed him steadfast love, so he took courage and gathered leaders to go with him (vv. 27–28).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. Ezra, priest and teacher, carried God’s law in his hand; Jesus is the Teacher who gave the law, kept it perfectly for us, and on the road to Emmaus “interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Yet a law carried in the hand, however well taught, could not change hearts, as the next chapters show. The chapter leaves us needing the new covenant, in which God says, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

For us. Ezra’s order is for every Christian: study God’s word, do it, then pass it on, to children, friends or a congregation. When doors open, bless God who opened them, and take courage from his hand, not from your own ability.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Hand of the LORD His God Was on Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s hand rests on the man who has given himself to God’s word. After nearly sixty years of silence in the story, Ezra is introduced by his ancestry, a priestly line running back through Zadok and Phinehas to Aaron (vv. 1–5), and by his skill as a scribe in the law of Moses (v. 6). The king grants him everything he asks, “for the hand of the LORD his God was on him”. A second company of Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants goes up with him in Artaxerxes’ seventh year (v. 7), arriving after four months on the road (vv. 8–9). The reason is given in verse 10: Ezra had set his heart to study the law, to do it and to teach it.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 explains verse 9: the good hand of God rested on the man who had set his heart on God's law, to study it, do it and teach it.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's family tree holds a surprise for anyone who has just read 2 Chronicles 34.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a long gap, Ezra is introduced as a true priest, descended from Aaron through the high-priestly line, and from the very family that once found the lost Book of the Law.

Now after this. Three words, and fifty-eight years go by. Everything in the book of Esther happens in the gap between chapter 6 and chapter 7. The house has stood for two generations, and most of the people who dedicated it are dead.

Son of Aaron the chief priest. The genealogy is not decoration: it shows that Ezra is a priest of the true line, traced back through Zadok and Phinehas to Aaron. The list skips generations, and “son of” means descendant. Seraiah, the first name, was the chief priest executed at Riblah in 586 (2 Kings 25:18–21), more than a century before Ezra’s journey. His son Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chronicles 6:15), and his grandson was Jeshua, who built the altar in chapter 3.

Son of Hilkiah. One name should stop a reader who has just come through 2 Chronicles. Hilkiah stands two generations above Seraiah (1 Chronicles 6:13–14): he is the high priest of Josiah’s reign, who, while the workmen were bringing money out of the temple, “found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses” (2 Chronicles 34:14).

The finder’s descendant. God’s word had been lost in God’s own house until Hilkiah found it. A century and a half later, the man who carries that same law back to Jerusalem to teach it to the whole nation is Hilkiah’s descendant. Families carry more than blood. Somewhere in that line, through an exile and a burned temple, somebody kept telling the children about the book.
verseByVerse.note: Ezra came almost sixty years after the temple was finished, in 458 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him. And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra was a master of God’s law, and the king gave him everything he asked because God’s hand was on him; with him went a second company of returning exiles.

A scribe skilled in the Law of Moses. A scribe was a trained writer and copyist, and in Ezra a scholar of the law. The psalmist has the picture: “my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe” (Psalm 45:1), using the same word for “skilled”. For Ezra the law of Moses was not a reference work but the language he thought in. His descent gave him his standing; his skill with the book gave him his usefulness.

The hand of the LORD his God was on him. “The hand of the LORD” appears six times in chapters 7 and 8 (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31), and every time it explains something that would not normally have happened. Why did the most powerful king on earth give a Jewish scribe everything he asked? Not because Ezra negotiated well, but because God’s hand was on him.

There went up also to Jerusalem. He did not go alone. Every order of the temple community is represented again, as in chapter 2: people of Israel, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants. It is a second return, smaller than the first, bringing what the first had lacked: a teacher of the law.

A scribe trained for the kingdom. Jesus spoke of “every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven”, who brings out of his treasure “what is new and what is old” (Matthew 13:52). Ezra brought out the old law; Christ’s scribes bring out the same Scriptures and show how they are fulfilled in him.

When did Ezra come? The traditional date is 458 BC, the seventh year of Artaxerxes I, thirteen years before Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:1). Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, putting Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah. But Ezra and Nehemiah appear together at the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:9) and at the dedication of the wall (Nehemiah 12:26, 36), which fits the traditional order best. The strongest argument for the later date is a name: Ezra spends a night in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib (10:6), and a high priest Johanan is known from papyri found at Elephantine in Egypt around 410 BC. But the name was common, and an earlier Jehohanan with a temple room is easily possible. This commentary takes the traditional date as the most natural reading (see the introduction), and nothing in the book’s message depends on settling it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king. For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him. For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
