Ezra’s long journey was brought safely to its end by God’s kind hand, and the reason the writer gives is that Ezra had given his heart to study God’s law, to obey it and to teach it.

On the first day of the first month. Four months and about nine hundred miles, with families, animals and a great deal of gold. He began on the first day of the first month, the day on which Moses was told to set up the tabernacle, and did (Exodus 40:2, 17). Whether Ezra chose the date for that reason we are not told, but a scribe who knew the law as he did could hardly have missed it. (The caravan actually left the river Ahava on the twelfth, after a halt to gather Levites and to fast; 8:31 gives that date.)

The good hand of his God was on him. Good, this time, not only powerful but kind. The hand that could have crushed a small party on the desert roads kept it instead.

For Ezra had set his heart. Verse 10, which this half of the book stands on, begins with “for”: it gives the reason for verse 9. This does not mean that Ezra’s diligence earned God’s favour; God’s hand was on Ezra long before. It means that the man who had given his life to God’s word is the man God’s hand rested on.

To study the Law of the LORD. “Set his heart” is the phrase that runs through 2 Chronicles, where a man either set his heart to seek God or did not (2 Chronicles 12:14; 30:19), and the word translated “study” is the Hebrew word for seeking. What is new here is the object: Ezra set his heart to seek the law. He looked for God where God had spoken.

To do it and to teach his statutes. The order is fixed: study it, do it, teach it. A man cannot honestly teach what he has not first obeyed, and he cannot obey what he has not first taken the trouble to understand. Most failures in the ministry of the word are failures to keep that order: teaching without studying, which produces nonsense, or teaching without doing, which produces hypocrites. James puts it plainly: “be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1:22).

Not only for preachers. Every parent teaches, and every believer is watched by someone. Is what I pass on something I have first sat down with, and then lived in? None of us keeps that order perfectly. The Spirit who opens minds to the Scriptures works it in us, and Christ, the Teacher Ezra points forward to, kept it perfectly in our place.

Uncertain wording. In verse 9 the Hebrew is compressed, literally that was the foundation of the going up. The ESV takes it to mean that Ezra began the journey that day; others read it as the day he fixed or ordered the departure. Either way the date of starting is the first of the first month.
verseByVerse.note: The journey took about four months.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–26 — The Law of Your God, Which Is in Your Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A Persian king sends Ezra with God’s law in his hand and the empire’s resources behind him. Artaxerxes lets any Israelite who freely offers go with Ezra, and sends him to examine Judah and Jerusalem by the law of his God (vv. 11–14). He sends silver and gold from himself, his counsellors, the province and the people, to buy sacrifices for the altar, and leaves the rest to Ezra’s judgment (vv. 15–20). The treasurers of the province must supply him generously, for the king fears the wrath of the God of heaven, and the temple staff are freed from tax (vv. 21–24). Ezra is to appoint judges who know God’s laws, and to teach those who do not (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The king's letter puts the law of God at the centre of Judah's life: the standard by which it is examined, the funding of its worship, and the teaching of its people.
verseByVerse.examples: Look for what the letter funds first, and what it frees from tax.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel: "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you. For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand, and also to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, with all the silver and gold that you shall find in the whole province of Babylonia, and with the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly for the house of their God that is in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s letter let any Israelite who wished go with Ezra, sent Ezra to examine Judah by God’s law, and gave him the gifts of the king, his counsellors and the people for God’s house.

A copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra. The letter, verses 12 to 26, is given in the Aramaic it was written in, and the narrator introduces it with a third description of Ezra in six verses: skilled (v. 6), set on the law (v. 10), “learned” in it (v. 11). The book will not let us forget what kind of man is being sent.

Artaxerxes, king of kings. This was the Persian emperor’s standard title. The man who styled himself king of kings is commissioning a scribe to teach the law of the God who really is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Revelation 19:16), a title Scripture finally gives to Christ.

Who freely offers to go to Jerusalem. Nobody is conscripted. As in chapter 1, the door is opened and people are left to walk through it.

The Law of your God, which is in your hand. Two hands meet in this chapter. The hand of the LORD was on Ezra (vv. 6, 9, 28); the law of the LORD was in Ezra’s hand (v. 14). The man God holds is the man who holds God’s word. The king understood that the scroll Ezra carried, not the king’s own laws or the customs of the province, was the standard by which Jerusalem was to be examined.

The king and his seven counselors. The book of Esther names that council, “the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14), and it was their advice, in the reign of this king’s father, that had Queen Vashti deposed by an unchangeable decree. A generation later the same body of men is voting gold for the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.note: Artaxerxes’ letter (vv. 12–26) is in Aramaic (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem. Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God. The vessels that have been given you for the service of the house of your God, you shall deliver before the God of Jerusalem. And whatever else is required for the house of your God, which it falls to you to provide, you may provide it out of the king's treasury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The money was to go first to the altar, and the king trusted Ezra and his brothers to spend the rest according to the will of their God.

Buy bulls, rams, and lambs. The first use of the money is the altar: before salaries or buildings, offerings. The king seems to have understood what the house was for.

According to the will of your God. Then an extraordinary grant of trust: “Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God.” No accounting to the treasury, no schedule of approved spending. In the spending of his own gift, the king was willing to be governed by a law he had never read.

Deliver before the God of Jerusalem. The vessels given for the house are to be delivered to God himself, and anything further the house requires, Ezra may draw from the royal treasury. It is Darius’s decree of chapter 6 renewed and enlarged by his grandson.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence, up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much. Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. We also notify you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on anyone of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the doorkeepers, the temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king ordered his treasurers to supply Ezra generously and freed the temple staff from tax, because he feared the wrath of Israel’s God.

Up to 100 talents of silver. A huge sum: a talent was about seventy-five pounds, so this is more than three tons of silver, set as an upper limit.

Salt without prescribing how much. The king sets no limit on the salt. The law required that every grain offering be seasoned with salt, “the salt of the covenant with your God” (Leviticus 2:13), and the king’s clerks, whether they knew it or not, wrote no ceiling on it.

Lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. The king’s motive is frank. Artaxerxes is afraid of Israel’s God. He does not worship him, but he does not want to be on the wrong side of him, and he is prepared to pay to stay on the right side. It is not faith, but it is more sense than many people have. There was probably policy in it too. Persian kings had local laws gathered and upheld in other provinces, and in these very years Egypt was in revolt against Persia, so a settled and loyal Judah on the road to Egypt was worth paying for.

Tribute, custom, or toll. Then the tax exemption for every servant of the house. These are the same three words the accusers of chapter 4 used to frighten this very king (4:13). Now they are written down as the things the servants of God’s house will never have to pay.

Religion as an insurance policy. Artaxerxes’ religion is more common than it looks. Plenty of people today keep a little God in reserve: they would not call themselves believers, but they pray before surgery, have the children christened, and would rather not be on the wrong side of whatever is up there. Religious people can do the same in a more respectable form, keeping the rules with care as a premium paid against disaster. Either way God is a power to be managed rather than a person to be loved, and the arrangement lasts as long as the payments do. The Bible has no quarrel with Artaxerxes’ fear; the God of heaven is to be feared. But it will not let anyone buy a place on his side. At the heart of the gospel the premium was paid in the other direction. We did not pay God to keep his wrath away. He paid, in his Son, to bear it himself, so that those “justified by his blood” are “saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9). What he wants in return is not a policyholder but a child.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach. Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra was commissioned to appoint judges who knew God’s law and to teach it to those who did not, with the king’s authority behind the law.

According to the wisdom of your God. In verse 14 the king called it the law of your God; here he calls it the wisdom of your God, and he means the same scroll. A Persian emperor has put it well: the law of God is not an arbitrary list of restrictions but his wisdom written down, and it can be carried in one man’s hand.

Those who do not know them, you shall teach. Ezra is to appoint judges from among those who already know God’s statutes, and to teach the rest. The Persian crown has written teaching into law. Four hundred years earlier Jehoshaphat had sent Levites round Judah “having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them” (2 Chronicles 17:9); now an emperor sends a scribe to do the same for a province stretching from the Euphrates to Egypt, though in practice it meant the Jews living there.

Let judgment be strictly executed on him. Verse 26 attaches penalties, death, banishment, confiscation or prison, to anyone who “will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king”. That is Persian civil enforcement, and it belongs to a particular moment when a community’s religious law was also its civil law under an imperial governor.

What it does not mean. It is not a pattern for the church, whose Lord gave it no sword and whose weapons, Paul says, “are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). The church teaches and disciplines its members, but it does not punish unbelief with the power of the state.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — Blessed Be the LORD, the God of Our Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra answers the king’s generosity by blessing God, who put it into the king’s heart. The memoir in Ezra’s own voice begins here, and its first words are praise. He sees the king’s favour as the LORD’s steadfast love shown to him before the whole court (vv. 27–28). Because the hand of the LORD his God was on him, he takes courage, not in his own ability or in the king’s letter, and does the next practical thing, gathering leading men of Israel to go up with him.
verseByVerse.theology: The letter was written by a king, the treasury was the king's, and the first thing Ezra does with it is give the credit away. God put the thing into the king's heart. God showed him steadfast love in front of the court. God's hand gave him courage. There is not a word here about his own qualifications, though the chapter has just spent five verses listing them.
verseByVerse.examples: At verse 27 the text changes language and voice at once. The king's letter was in Aramaic; Ezra's blessing is in Hebrew, and in the first person. From here to the end of chapter 9 the book is Ezra's own account, in his own words.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra blessed God for turning the king’s heart and for showing him steadfast love, and, strengthened by God’s hand, he gathered leaders to go with him.

Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers. Here Ezra’s own account begins, in the first person, and its first words are a blessing. He has just been handed the most generous commission in the book, sealed by the king of kings, and he does not admire the king for it. He blesses the God “who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king”. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1), and Ezra knows whose hand turned it, as it had turned Cyrus’s (1:1).

Extended to me his steadfast love. Steadfast love, hesed, the covenant love the singers sang over the foundation in chapter 3, is shown to one man in a room full of Persian officials. God’s faithfulness to his people did not stop at the border of the promised land.

I took courage. The word is used of a man bracing himself, as Jehoiada “took courage” before he acted (2 Chronicles 23:1). Ezra did not feel brave because the letter was generous. He took courage because of whose hand was on him, and then he did the next practical thing, which was to gather people.

A shadow of a greater Teacher. The scribe who set his heart to study the law, do it and teach it was a gift to his generation, and a shadow of someone greater: a Teacher who did not need to study the law, because he had given it; who did it perfectly, in the place of all who have not; and who, on the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets … interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself”, and then “opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:27, 45). Ezra carried the book in his hand. The book is about Jesus.

7.theology: Verse 10 is the heart of the second half of Ezra, and every ministry of the word stands or falls by keeping its order: study, then do, then teach. God’s hand is on Ezra and God’s law is in his hand, and Ezra gives God the credit for every open door: the king was generous because God put it into his heart (v. 27).
7.examples: The whole story of Esther happens between the last verse of chapter 6 and the first verse of chapter 7. Then a descendant of the priest who found the lost Book of the Law carries it back to Jerusalem, setting out on the day the tabernacle was first set up, with a Persian decree ordering that those who do not know God's law be taught it.

keyVerse.quote: For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.
keyVerse.note: The second half of the book stands on this verse. It explains why God’s good hand rested on Ezra, and it sets the order for every ministry of the word: study, then do, then teach. Parents, friends and preachers alike can only pass on well what they have first understood and lived.

7.reflection:
Somewhere in Hilkiah’s family line, through exile and a burned temple, someone kept telling the children about God’s word (vv. 1–5). Who passed the faith on to you, and to whom are you passing it on?

Ezra set his heart to study the law, to do it and to teach it, in that order (v. 10). Which of the three do you find hardest, and what happens when the order is reversed?

Artaxerxes paid generously to keep on the right side of Israel’s God (v. 23). In what ways are we tempted to treat God as a power to be managed rather than a Father to be loved, and how does the gospel answer that?

Ezra blessed God, not the king, for the king’s generosity, and took courage because God’s hand was on him (vv. 27–28). Where has God opened a door for you recently, and how can you give him the credit and act on it?

8.title: The Journey of Faith: Fasting, Prayer, and the Treasure Carried to Jerusalem
8.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush.<sup>3</sup>Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men.<sup>4</sup>Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.<sup>5</sup>Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men.<sup>7</sup>Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men.<sup>8</sup>Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men.<sup>9</sup>Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men.<sup>10</sup>Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men.<sup>11</sup>Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men.<sup>12</sup>Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.<sup>13</sup>Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men.<sup>14</sup>Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.<sup>15</sup>I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi.<sup>16</sup>Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight,<sup>17</sup>and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God.<sup>18</sup>And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18;<sup>19</sup>also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20;<sup>20</sup>besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.<sup>21</sup>Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods.<sup>22</sup>For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him."<sup>23</sup>So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.<sup>24</sup>Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them.<sup>25</sup>And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered.<sup>26</sup>I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold,<sup>27</sup>20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold.<sup>28</sup>And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.<sup>29</sup>Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.<sup>31</sup>Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way.<sup>32</sup>We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.<sup>33</sup>On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui.<sup>34</sup>The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.<sup>35</sup>At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>36</sup>They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
8.overview:
Where we are. Ezra has the king’s letter and has blessed God for it (7:27–28). Now, speaking in his own voice, he tells how he gathered the company, prepared for the journey and brought them and the treasure safely to Jerusalem in 458 BC.

The message. God’s good hand brings his people home, and those who trust him live and work as if that is true. Ezra will not ask for soldiers after telling the king that God protects those who seek him, so he fasts and prays instead, and God brings the caravan through ambushes on the road. The same faith that refuses an escort also counts every ounce of gold, because holy things deserve honest handling.

Why it was said. The first readers needed to know that God still protected and provided for his people under foreign rule, and that faith and careful administration belong together (see the introduction). They also needed to see that latecomers belonged and every tribe still counted.

How the chapter makes its case. Ezra lists the families who went with him, among them a son of David and the latecomers of families who went home eighty years before (vv. 1–14). At the river Ahava he finds no Levites, sends a carefully briefed delegation, and by God’s good hand ministers come (vv. 15–20). Ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, he proclaims a fast, and God listens (vv. 21–23). He weighs the treasure out to priests and Levites, holy men to guard holy things (vv. 24–30). God brings them safely through (vv. 31–32); in Jerusalem everything is weighed and recorded, offerings are made for all Israel, and the king’s orders are delivered (vv. 33–36).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Hattush, a son of David with no throne, walks in this caravan, carrying the promise of an everlasting kingdom toward the Son of David who would receive it (Luke 1:32–33). And Ezra’s gold arriving complete because God’s hand was on it is a picture of the Good Shepherd, who says of his people, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). Paul joined the chapter’s two words, ashamed and guard: “I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (2 Timothy 1:12).

For us. When you have said in front of others that God can be trusted, live as though it is true, and take your remaining fears to him in prayer. Handle what belongs to God honestly and carefully. And trust Christ to bring you, with everything you have entrusted to him, safely home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — I Found There None of the Sons of Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gathers the people and the ministers his work needs. Ezra names the families who travelled with him: priests of Phinehas and Ithamar, Hattush of the house of David, and twelve lay families, most of them branches of families that had gone home with Zerubbabel eighty years before (vv. 1–14). When he reviews the company at the river Ahava he finds not one Levite (v. 15). Rather than go without them, he sends a delegation of leading men to Iddo at Casiphia, telling them exactly what to say (vv. 16–17). “By the good hand of our God on us” Levites come, Sherebiah and Hashabiah with their kinsmen, and two hundred and twenty temple servants, every one named (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The shortage of Levites seen at 2:40 has not gone away in eighty years. Ezra did not set off without Levites and hope for the best; he stopped the caravan and went and asked.
verseByVerse.examples: Some families take two journeys to get home, and some of the people who join a work of God at the last minute become its mainstays.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king: Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush. Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men. Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men. Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men. Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men. Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men. Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men. Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men. Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men. Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men. Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men. Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men. Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra lists the families who travelled with him: priests, a descendant of David, and the latecomers of families whose cousins had gone home eighty years before.

Who went up with me. The list is Ezra’s own: the people he travelled with, whose names he knew.

Of the sons of David, Hattush. First come the priests, Gershom of the line of Phinehas and Daniel of the line of Ithamar, and then a name that matters. First Chronicles places Hattush several generations down from Zerubbabel (1 Chronicles 3:19–22). The house of David has no throne and no kingdom, but it has a member walking in this caravan, and somebody still knew exactly whose descendant he was.

Twelve lay families. Then twelve lay families, each head named and its men counted. They come to 1,496 men, with wives and children besides, a small company beside the forty-two thousand of chapter 2.

Branches that stayed behind. Almost every family name here is a family name from chapter 2. The sons of Parosh, of Pahath-moab, of Zattu, of Adin, of Elam: their cousins went home with Zerubbabel eighty years before. These are the branches that stayed behind, and now, two or three generations later, they are following. Some families take two journeys to get home.

Those who came later. The text says so itself at verse 13. Six hundred and sixty-six of Adonikam’s family went home with Zerubbabel (2:13). The rest, Eliphelet, Jeuel, Shemaiah and sixty men, are described as what they were: the ones who came later. God’s timetable for a family is not always the same for every member of it.

The promise on the road. The promise that David’s house would stand for ever (2 Samuel 7:16) was being carried, without a crown, along a desert road toward the Son of David in whom it would be kept: “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32).

Textual note. Zattu and Bani in verses 5 and 10 are missing from the Hebrew and supplied from the Septuagint; a word had probably dropped out in copying.

verseByVerse.quote: I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi. Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight, and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God. And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18; also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20; besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding no Levites in the company, Ezra stopped, sent a carefully briefed delegation to ask for ministers, and by God’s good hand Levites and temple servants came.

I found there none of the sons of Levi. There was not a single Levite in the caravan. It is the problem of chapter 2 in a sharper form: the first return had brought seventy-four Levites to more than four thousand priests (2:36–40), and this one had brought nobody at all. The men whose work was the carrying, the cleaning, the slaughtering and the teaching, the daily, heavy, unglamorous service of the house (Numbers 3:5–8; see Priests and Levites), had settled in Babylon and were not coming.

Then I sent for Eliezer. Ezra could have gone without them. He stopped instead, and sent eleven envoys, three of them called Elnathan, which says something about the popular names of that generation, “to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia”.

Telling them what to say. He told them exactly what to say. A request for ministers is too important to leave to improvisation.

Namely Sherebiah. Levites came, and the first one named is Sherebiah, “a man of discretion”. Remember the name. Years later, when Ezra read the law aloud to the city, Levites went among the crowd and “helped the people to understand the Law” (Nehemiah 8:7), and Sherebiah is on that list. The man fetched at the last minute went on to explain the book.

The temple servants. The temple servants came too, “whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites”. This order went back five hundred years to David’s organising of the house, and it still answered when called.

By the good hand of our God on us. Ezra does not credit his own recruiting. The people who join a work of God are also his gift, and the Lord of the harvest still sends out labourers when his people ask him (Matthew 9:38).

Uncertain wording. Casiphia is mentioned nowhere else, and its location is unknown. It was probably a settlement of exiles not far from Babylon where a community of Levites and temple servants lived under Iddo. Ezra twice calls it “the place”, a word sometimes used of a sanctuary, so some think there was a centre of worship or teaching there; that cannot be proved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–23 — I Was Ashamed to Ask the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith that has spoken in public must be lived in private. Ezra proclaims a fast at the river Ahava so that the company may humble themselves before God and seek a safe journey for themselves, their children and their goods (v. 21). He was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen, because he had told the king that God’s good hand is on all who seek him and his wrath against all who forsake him (v. 22). So they fasted and pleaded with God, and he listened to their entreaty (v. 23). The passage shows integrity under pressure, and the humble prayer that carries the fears that remain once a decision of faith has been made.
verseByVerse.theology: Ezra had told a Persian emperor what God does for those who seek him. Having said it, he had to travel as though it were true.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra is honest enough to write that he was ashamed: not of trusting God, but of being seen to contradict himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods. For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him." So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having told the king that God protects those who seek him, Ezra would not ask for soldiers; instead the company fasted and prayed for a safe journey, and God heard them.

That we might humble ourselves. To humble themselves and seek echoes the promise God gave at the dedication of the first temple: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face” (2 Chronicles 7:14). They had a nine-hundred-mile road ahead, children, and a fortune in gold. They went on their faces by the canal.

For I was ashamed. Ezra was ashamed, but not of God, and he was not too proud to ask for help. He had told the Persian court that his God protects those who seek him. To ask for cavalry a few weeks later would have told the king that Ezra did not really believe it.

Seek and forsake. These are the two great verbs of 2 Chronicles, joined by the prophet Azariah: “If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you” (2 Chronicles 15:2). Ezra had preached the message of that whole book to a pagan emperor; now he had to travel as though it were true.

He listened to our entreaty. It is the word used when God “was moved by his entreaty” in the prayer of Manasseh in chains (2 Chronicles 33:13). The God who let himself be entreated by the worst king in Judah let himself be entreated by a frightened scribe beside a canal.

Faith that has spoken aloud. Most believers know this kind of faith: the faith that has said something out loud, in front of people who are watching, and now has to live up to it. The words were easy at court. They were harder at the edge of the desert with the children loaded on the donkeys.

What fasting is. Many people hear the word and think of a diet, a protest, or a way of twisting God’s arm: if I go without, he will have to listen. Ezra gives another reason: “that we might humble ourselves before our God”. To fast is to say with the body what the mouth can say too glibly: I need you more than I need my next meal. For a day it takes away the comfortable feeling that we can manage, and Ezra, with Persian cavalry only a request away, knew how strong that feeling is. Nor did the hunger buy the safe road. God listened, and that was mercy, not wages.

The one who lived on his Father’s word. Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness and answered the tempter, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). He truly lived on his Father’s word, and he took it for granted that his people would fast: “when you fast”, he said (Matthew 6:17), and once the bridegroom was taken away, “then they will fast” (Matthew 9:15). So before a decision that frightens you, try missing one meal and spending that hour telling God plainly what you are afraid of. Every pang is a reminder of whom you are leaning on.

What it does not mean. This is not a rule that faith refuses soldiers or other ordinary protection. Nehemiah, sent by the same king thirteen years later, travelled with “officers of the army and horsemen” (Nehemiah 2:9), and nobody rebukes him. Ezra’s case was particular: he had said a particular thing, and integrity required him to stand on it. So he did what faithful people do with the fear that remains after they have made their decision. He took it to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–36 — The Weight of Everything Was Recorded
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Holy things are guarded, counted and accounted for, and God brings them home. Ezra weighs out the immense treasure, silver, gold and precious vessels, to twelve leading priests and to Levites, telling them that they and the vessels are holy to the LORD and that all of it must be weighed again in Jerusalem (vv. 24–30). The hand of God delivers them from the enemy and from ambushes on the road (vv. 31–32). In the house of God everything is weighed and recorded, and nothing is missing (vv. 33–34). The returned exiles offer burnt offerings and sin offerings for all Israel, and the king’s orders are delivered to the officials, who now help the people and the house of God (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology: Holy people carry holy things, and have them weighed at the other end. Being holy does not excuse anyone from giving an account.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 31 does not say there were no enemies; it says God delivered them from the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them. And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered. I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold, 20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold. And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers. Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD." So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra entrusted the huge treasure to priests and Levites, telling them that they and the vessels were holy to the LORD, and that every item must be weighed again in Jerusalem.

Twelve of the leading priests. A careful reader will stop here, because Sherebiah and Hashabiah were introduced six verses ago as Levites, not priests, and verse 30 says it was “the priests and the Levites” who took charge of the treasure. The likeliest sense is that Ezra appointed twelve leading priests and, alongside them, these two Levites with ten of their kinsmen, priests and Levites sharing the charge. The rest of the passage requires it.

I weighed out to them. The figures are enormous: 650 talents of silver, about twenty-two tonnes, silver vessels worth two hundred talents, a hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics, and “two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold”. All of it was to be carried nine hundred miles without an escort.

You are holy to the LORD. The men and the metal were both set apart, both belonging to God.

Guard them and keep them. Then comes the most practical sentence imaginable: guard them and keep them “until you weigh them”. Weighed out at Ahava, weighed in at Jerusalem. The holiness of the trust did not make the accounting unnecessary. It made it essential.

For anyone who handles God’s things. Anyone who handles what belongs to God, money given for his work, the care of his people, the teaching of his word, should hear both halves in that order. First, you are holy to the LORD, set apart by him and not by your own diligence; then, it will be weighed at the other end.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “fine bright” is rare, and its exact sense is not known; it may mean gleaming or golden-coloured, perhaps a fine alloy. Either way the two bronze vessels were valued as highly as gold.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds and a daric about 1/4 ounce (ESV notes): 650 talents of silver is over 24 tons.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answered the prayer at Ahava by bringing the caravan safely through the ambushes on the road, not by removing every enemy from it.

From the river Ahava. Verse 31 tells four months of road in one honest sentence. Robbers lay in wait for a caravan carrying more than twenty tonnes of silver, and they got nothing.

The hand of our God was on us. Two hands are in the verse: the hand of our God on us, and the hand of the enemy against us, and God’s proved the stronger. That hand is now named six times in two chapters: on Ezra before the king, on him for the road, on him when he took courage, on the caravan when the Levites came, for good on all who seek him, and on the road (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31).

How God answers prayer for protection. That is usually how God answers the prayer for protection: not by removing every threat from the road, but by bringing his people through the threats. A believer who expects the first will be disillusioned; a believer who expects the second will find it true. “The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore” (Psalm 121:8).

There we remained three days. After four months they rested three days before doing anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui. The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house of God the whole treasure was weighed and recorded, received by priests and Levites, and nothing was missing.

Weighed into the hands of Meremoth. Four named men received it, two priests and two Levites, just as priests and Levites together had carried it.

Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah. Nehemiah gives his descent: “Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz” (Nehemiah 3:4). When the first returnees arrived eighty years earlier, the sons of Hakkoz could not find their registration and were barred from the priesthood “until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim”, the sacred lots for seeking God’s answer (2:61–63).

A name found again. Now a son of Hakkoz is called “Meremoth the priest”, standing in the house of God with the treasure weighed into his hands. The text does not tell us how the question was settled. It simply shows the family that could not find its name in the register entrusted, eighty years later, with the gold of the house. They had been shut out only until God’s answer could be sought, and the door had opened.

The weight of everything was recorded. Twenty-two tonnes of silver, more than three tonnes of gold, the bowls and the bronze, carried nine hundred miles past ambushes, came out right on the scales in the house of God. Nothing was missing, and the fact was written down.

Accounts and the honour of God. Paul took pains with the collection he carried to Jerusalem “so that no one should blame us about this generous gift” (2 Corinthians 8:20). Ezra had the same instinct five centuries earlier. The honour of God was bound up with the honesty of the men carrying his gold, and churches today still owe him open, checked accounts.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD. They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new arrivals offered sacrifices for all twelve tribes, and the king’s orders were delivered to his officials, who now helped the people and the house of God.

Twelve bulls for all Israel. Twelve bulls and twelve goats for all Israel, and ninety-six rams, eight for each tribe. Like the returnees of chapter 6 (6:17), this company offers for every tribe, though it came from only a few. They would not let Israel shrink to the size of whoever had made the journey, and the sin offering pointed to the one sacrifice that would gather a people from every tribe and nation.

The king’s satraps. A satrap governed one of the great regions into which Persia divided its lands, and “the province Beyond the River” was the region west of the Euphrates, Judah included. Delivering the king’s commissions put Artaxerxes’ letter into force: the treasurers were to supply Ezra, and no tax was to be laid on the servants of the house (7:21–24). The officials who in this king’s reign had once stopped the building of the city (4:23) now “aided the people and the house of God”.

Two words that belong together. At Ahava, Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for protection, because he had said God would guard those who seek him. And he told the priests to guard the treasure until it was weighed in Jerusalem. Five centuries later, writing from prison with his life nearly spent, the apostle Paul put both words in one sentence: “But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (2 Timothy 1:12). Ezra’s gold came out right on the scales because God’s hand was on the caravan. Everything a believer has entrusted to Christ will come out right on the last day for the same reason: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

8.theology:
The fast at Ahava is what integrity looks like once words of faith have been said in public, and the answer to it shows that God protects his people by bringing them through danger, not by keeping all danger away (v. 31).

Verses 24-34 bind holiness to accountability: the more sacred a trust, the more carefully it is counted.
8.examples: There was not one Levite in the caravan, so Ezra stopped and sent to ask, and three of the eleven men he sent were called Elnathan. A fortune in silver then travelled nine hundred miles past ambushes and came out right on the scales in the house of God.

keyVerse.quote: For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, “The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him.”
keyVerse.note: This verse shows faith that has spoken in public choosing to live by what it said. Ezra’s confidence in God’s good hand is the theme of chapters 7 and 8, and here it is tested on the edge of the desert. It leads straight to the fast, the prayer and the safe arrival that follow.

8.reflection:
Many in Ezra’s caravan belonged to families whose cousins had gone home eighty years earlier: “those who came later” (v. 13). How does this encourage you about family members who have not yet come to Christ?

Ezra would not go on without Levites, and he told his messengers exactly what to say (vv. 15–17). What gaps in our church’s ministry should make us stop and pray and ask, rather than press on without them?

Ezra was ashamed to ask for soldiers after telling the king that God protects those who seek him (v. 22). Where have you said something about God in front of others that you now have to live up to? How can prayer and fasting help?

The treasure was holy, and so it was weighed out, guarded and weighed in again (vv. 24–34). What does faithful, accountable handling of God’s things look like in your life and in our church?

9.title: Ezra's Great Prayer: Intercessory Identification and the Gravity of Sin
9.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites.<sup>2</sup>For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."<sup>3</sup>As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled.<sup>4</sup>Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice.<sup>5</sup>And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,<sup>6</sup>saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens.<sup>7</sup>From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.<sup>8</sup>But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery.<sup>9</sup>For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>"And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments,<sup>11</sup>which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness.<sup>12</sup>Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'<sup>13</sup>And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this,<sup>14</sup>shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape?<sup>15</sup>O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
9.overview:
Where we are. Ezra has reached Jerusalem, the treasure weighed and the king’s letters delivered (8:31–36). His memoir now turns from the journey to the people, and from the house of God to the hearts of its worshippers.

The message. God’s people have gone back to the sin that sent them into exile, and the right response begins not with a plan but with honest confession before a God who has been kinder than they deserved. We have forsaken him, yet he has not forsaken us. And Ezra stops where every honest sinner must: no one can stand before a just God, and the answer is his to give.

Why it was said. The remnant lived in a small, poor province among neighbours whose gods had once filled the land (see the introduction), and marrying into those households looked like ordinary good sense. The chapter shows how God sees it: not as a social matter but as faithlessness, the old road to the old ruin.

How the chapter makes its case. Officials report that people, priests and Levites, with the leaders foremost, have married into households that serve other gods (vv. 1–2). Ezra tears his clothes, pulls out his own hair and sits appalled until the evening sacrifice, and those who tremble at God’s word come and sit with him (vv. 3–5). Then he prays. He is ashamed for “our iniquities”, though he did not share them, and sets the present sin inside the whole history of judgment (vv. 6–7). He thanks God for a brief moment of favour, a tent-peg in his holy place and a little reviving (vv. 8–9). He confesses that they have broken the commandments again, after mercy beyond their deserving (vv. 10–14). And he ends with a verdict, “you are just”, and no request at all (v. 15).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. Ezra, confessing sins he had not committed as if they were his own, is a faint picture of the one Intercessor who did more than say “we”: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). And the prayer stops at “none can stand before you”, the very place where Psalm 130:3 asks, “who could stand?” The next verse answers, “But with you there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:4), and God can say it without injustice only because at the cross Christ stood where the guilty could not stand. In him we stand (Romans 5:2).

For us. Take sin seriously enough to grieve over it, your own and your church’s, before you reach for a solution. Say “we”, not “they”. And when your guilt seems higher than your head, do not bargain: agree with God, and trust the mercy he has already shown in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin among God’s people is first a cause for grief before God, not a problem to be managed. The officials report that people, priests and Levites have married into the households of the peoples of the land, the peoples named in the law, and that the leaders have led the way (vv. 1–2). The issue is whose gods a household serves, not its ancestry. Ezra calls no meeting and punishes no one. He tears his clothes, pulls out his own hair and sits appalled, and those who tremble at God’s words gather round him until the evening sacrifice, when he kneels and spreads out his hands to pray (vv. 3–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The list in verse 1 is the law's list, the nations of Deuteronomy 7:1 with Ammon, Moab and Egypt from Deuteronomy 23:3-7, and the law's reason goes with it: the concern was a household's worship, not its ancestry.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra’s first response to sin in the community is grief, not a plan of action.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Officials report that God’s people, led by their own leaders, have married into households that worship other gods: the very sin the law forbade and the exile punished.

After these things had been done. Ezra has been in Jerusalem some months, his commission under way (8:33–36), when the officials bring the worst news he could hear.

From the Canaanites, the Hittites. Several peoples on the list had not existed as nations for centuries. This is the law’s list: the nations of Deuteronomy 7:1, with the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians of Deuteronomy 23:3–8. The officials describe their neighbours in the vocabulary of the Torah; somebody had been reading the book Ezra brought.

The holy race. The ESV’s footnote gives the Hebrew as “offspring”, or seed. It echoes Isaiah’s picture of the stump left standing when the tree of Israel was cut down: “The holy seed is its stump” (Isaiah 6:13). The remnant was the seed God had kept alive for the future, and now that seed was being mixed in with the peoples around it.

What the problem was: worship, not race. Get this wrong and this chapter and the next will be badly misread. The law that forbade these marriages gave its reason in the same breath: “for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). Moabites are on the officials’ list, yet Ruth the Moabite became the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:17), because she said to Naomi, “your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16). Three chapters earlier the Passover was eaten by “every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land” (6:21). The door was open to anyone who came to the LORD. What the officials reported was the reverse: Israelites marrying into households that kept their gods.

The hand of the officials. The worst line comes last: “in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost.” The leaders had led. The men who should have guarded the fence were the first to break it.

Marriage for a Christian today. This does not mean that marriage across a line of race or nation is wrong: Moses himself married a Cushite woman, and God rebuked those who spoke against him over it (Numbers 12:1–9). What carries over is the reason Deuteronomy gave, worship. A believer belongs to the Lord who bought him, and is free to marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39), because marriage is a shared life before God. For those already married to someone who does not share their faith, the next chapter raises the hard question, and the apostle’s answer is plain: stay, and love (1 Corinthians 7:12–16; see the note on 10:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled. Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice. And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra’s first response to his people’s sin is not a plan but grief, and when the hour of sacrifice comes he turns that grief into prayer.

I tore my garment and my cloak. Ezra called no committee, ordered no inquiry and issued no statement. He tore both layers of his clothes, the familiar sign of mourning, pulled out hair from his own head and beard, and sat unable to move.

Ezra and Nehemiah compared. Nehemiah met the same sin a generation later: “I confronted them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair” (Nehemiah 13:25). Nehemiah pulled out other people’s hair; Ezra pulled out his own. Both were rightly grieved, and there is a place for Nehemiah’s kind of reformer, but Ezra’s first instinct was not to punish the guilty but to sit down in the dust beside them.

All who trembled. Those who “trembled at the words of the God of Israel” are the people to whom God says he looks: “he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:2). Nobody organised them; when a leader sits down in grief over sin, they come and sit with him.

At the evening sacrifice. He waited until the evening sacrifice, so that his confession of guilt rose while the lamb was on the altar. By the first century that afternoon offering had become “the hour of prayer, the ninth hour” (Acts 3:1).

Fell upon my knees. Then he knelt and spread out his hands, as Solomon did at the dedication of the first temple: “he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven” (2 Chronicles 6:13). Solomon asked God to hear the prayers of a sinning people turned toward that house (2 Chronicles 6:36–39). Ezra kneels at the rebuilt house to pray just such a prayer.

The ninth hour. Many Christians have noticed that it was at the ninth hour that Jesus, bearing sins that were not his own, cried out, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Ezra grieved at the hour of sacrifice for sins he had not committed; Christ, at that same hour, was the sacrifice for them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — None Can Stand Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honest confession sets the people’s sin beside God’s mercy and leaves the outcome to him. Ezra is ashamed for “our iniquities”, the sins of the whole people from the days of the fathers until now (vv. 6–7). Yet God has shown a brief moment of favour: a remnant, a tent-peg in his holy place, a little reviving even in slavery, because he has not forsaken them (vv. 8–9). They have forsaken his commandments, given through the law and the prophets, and done it again after being punished less than they deserved (vv. 10–14). The prayer ends with a verdict, “you are just”, and no request: “none can stand before you” (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer moves from shame, through thanks for a little reviving, to confession and a verdict, and at its centre a people who had forsaken God again confess that he had not forsaken them.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the prayer does not contain: no petition, no proposal, no bargain.

verseByVerse.quote: saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens. From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra confesses his people’s sin as his own, and sets it inside the whole history of Israel’s guilt and God’s judgment.

I am ashamed. It is the word Ezra used at the river Ahava, when he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers (8:22). There his shame was before a pagan emperor. Here it is before God, and for sins he did not commit.

Our iniquities. Watch the pronouns: “I am ashamed”, then in the same breath “our iniquities”, “our guilt”. Ezra had been in the country a few months and was not among the guilty. He could have said “their iniquities”, and never once does: from first sentence to last, the guilty party is “we”. That is intercession: not a righteous man reporting other people’s failings to God, but a man standing so close to the people he serves that before the throne he cannot tell their sin from his own.

Higher than our heads. The picture is a flood: iniquities risen over the head, guilt mounted up to the heavens. Sin here is not a list of separate offences to be ticked off one by one; it is water rising over a drowning man.

As it is today. He sets the present sin inside the whole history. The exile was not bad luck but God’s judgment on this same pattern of sin, and the people standing in Jerusalem are its survivors. A man who confesses only the latest sin has not understood the sin.

The one who carried it. The gospel goes further than Ezra could. Jesus did not merely say “we” about sins that were not his: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).

Why should I confess what I did not do? We are of two minds about this prayer. As individualists we answer only for our own choices, and to say “our iniquities” about sins I did not commit sounds theatrical, even unhealthy. Yet public life is full of collective guilt, nations apologising for their past and movements naming the sins of whole groups; but notice whose sins usually get confessed: the other side’s. The individualist says “not me”; the campaigner too often says “them”. Both stand outside the guilt looking in. Ezra stands inside a guilt he did not commit, without excusing himself and without pointing at anyone. That comes not from low self-esteem but from knowing that he too lives only by mercy (v. 8). People who have been carried as Christ carries us no longer need to be the innocent party, and can say “we” without despair.

verseByVerse.quote: But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery. For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of his confession Ezra thanks God for a small but real mercy: a remnant, a foothold and a little new life, because God has not forsaken his people even in their bondage.

But now. Mid-confession the prayer turns to grace, for we see how serious sin is only when we see how great the mercy was.

For a brief moment. Eighty years had passed since Cyrus’s decree, and to Ezra it was a brief moment: a breath of mercy after centuries of judgment.

A secure hold within his holy place. The ESV footnote gives the Hebrew as “nail, or tent-pin”: something driven into the ground that will take a rope and hold. The remnant had not been given a palace in God’s holy place, only a peg, a foothold, a place to fasten to. That was enough to hang a life on.

Brighten our eyes … a little reviving. The eyes of a starving man, or a man in the dark, brightening; a little life coming back into dead limbs. Not a great restoration. Every phrase is modest, and every phrase is gratitude.

For we are slaves. They were still subjects of Persia, paying its tribute in a province of its empire. The return had not ended their bondage.

Our God has not forsaken us. Hold that sentence, because the next verse says the people did the opposite: they forsook him. His “steadfast love” is covenant loyalty, which keeps its promises when the other party has not; here it reached them through “the kings of Persia”, who never knew whose love they carried.

Protection in Judea and Jerusalem. The ESV note gives the Hebrew as “a wall”. Jerusalem’s walls still lay in ruins; Nehemiah would rebuild them thirteen years later. Ezra thanks God for a wall that did not yet stand in stone, because God himself had already been their protection.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “protection” (gādēr) usually means the wall or fence round a vineyard or field rather than a city’s fortifications, and it is not certain whether Ezra has any literal wall in mind. Most take it as a picture: God had fenced his people round with safety, through the favour of the Persian kings. That is the likeliest meaning, and it fits the modest images of the verse before.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments, which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness. Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all God’s mercy there is nothing left to say but the truth: we have forsaken the commandments he gave, the very commandments that forbade these marriages.

What shall we say after this? Ezra runs out of words. After the mercy of the last two verses there is nothing to say but the truth.

For we have forsaken your commandments. Set this beside the verse before: “our God has not forsaken us” (v. 9); “we have forsaken your commandments” (v. 10). The two sentences stand side by side in the prayer, and the contrast between them is the whole story of grace.

Against the rule of Chronicles. Readers of 2 Chronicles know the rule these two verbs usually follow. The prophet Azariah stated it to Asa: “if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you” (2 Chronicles 15:2). By that rule a people who forsook God should have been forsaken. Ezra confesses that they had forsaken him, and that he had not forsaken them. The rule had been broken, from God’s side, in mercy.

A land impure. What Ezra quotes is not one verse but a summary of what the whole law says. “A land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands” is the language of Leviticus, where the land itself became unclean and “vomited out its inhabitants” (Leviticus 18:24–25). “Do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons” is Deuteronomy 7:3. “Never seek their peace or prosperity” is Deuteronomy 23:6, said of the Ammonites and the Moabites, both on the officials’ list.

By your servants the prophets. He attributes all of it to the prophets, and Moses was the first of them. The law and the prophets spoke with one voice about a household’s worship, and the people had heard it and done the opposite.

That you may be strong. The commandment was a fence to keep blessing in, not out: “that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.” God’s prohibitions guard a people’s faith, and their children’s.

verseByVerse.quote: And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this, shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape? O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Punished less than they deserved, they have committed the same sin again, and Ezra can only agree that God is just and that no one can stand before him.

Less than our iniquities deserved. The exile was terrible, the burned city, the dead, the seventy years, and Ezra says it was less than they deserved. “He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10). Having been let off so lightly, they had gone straight back to the sin that caused it. “Again” is the word that breaks him.

Would you not be angry with us? Ezra is not asking for effect. God would be within his rights to finish them, and Ezra knows it.

You are just. It is the confession Rehoboam and his princes made when Shishak was at the gates, “The LORD is righteous” (2 Chronicles 12:6), the first time in 2 Chronicles that anyone humbled himself. A confession that begins by agreeing with God’s verdict is the kind God has always heard.

A prayer without a request. There the prayer ends. He does not ask God to forgive them, spare them, or show them what to do; he lays the guilt before a just God, says nobody can stand, and stops. It is the exact place where a psalm pauses: “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (Psalm 130:3). Ezra reached that sentence and did not presume to say the next. He left it to God.

The answer God gives. God has said it: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). And he can say it without being unjust because of Jesus, who at the hour of the evening prayer stood where Ezra’s people could not stand, carried iniquities that had risen higher than all our heads, and was forsaken so that we would not be. So what was impossible is now true: “through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand” (Romans 5:2). None could stand. In him, we stand.

9.theology:
Ezra confesses sins he did not commit, in the first person plural, from the first sentence to the last. That is intercession, pleading with God for others, and it points forward to Christ, the one Intercessor, who bore sins that were not his.

Verses 9-10 put the gospel in two sentences: God has not forsaken a people who had forsaken him. And the prayer stops at none can stand before you, leaving God to give the answer, which in Christ he has.
9.examples: Nehemiah pulled out other people's hair over this sin; Ezra pulled out his own. Nobody organised the people who trembled at God's word; they came and sat down with him. He was not among the guilty, and he never once said their sin, and he thanked God for a wall thirteen years before Nehemiah built one.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this.
keyVerse.note: The whole prayer drives to this verdict. Ezra agrees with God against himself and his people, asks for nothing, and admits that no one can stand. That is where honest confession must arrive, and it is where the gospel begins: the God who is just has provided in Christ the one in whom sinners can stand (Romans 5:2).

9.reflection:
Ezra’s first response to the news was grief, not a plan (vv. 3–5). Why do we so often skip grief and go straight to fixing, blaming or managing? What would it look like to grieve first over sin in your church or family?

Ezra never says “their sin”, only “our iniquities” (v. 6), though he had not shared it. Where do you find it easier to stand outside the guilt and point? How does knowing that Christ carried sins not his own free you to say “we”?

Verses 9 and 10 set side by side “our God has not forsaken us” and “we have forsaken your commandments”. How does seeing God’s mercy clearly make sin look more serious, not less?

The prayer ends with no request, only “you are just” and “none can stand before you” (v. 15). What does Psalm 130:3–4 add, and what difference does it make to come to God with nothing to offer but Christ?

10.title: The Covenant Renewal: Painful Obedience and the Long Work of Reform
10.text: <sup>1</sup>While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children, gathered to him out of Israel, for the people wept bitterly.<sup>2</sup>And Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: "We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this.<sup>3</sup>Therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Law.<sup>4</sup>Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it."<sup>5</sup>Then Ezra arose and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath that they would do as had been said.
