10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 ended with Ezra on his knees, confessing the people’s faithlessness and asking for nothing (9:15). This last chapter tells what happened while he was still praying.

The message. Real repentance names sin honestly, still hopes in God, and then acts, even when acting is costly and slow. “Even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this” (v. 2): the hope rests not on the reform but on the God who kept a remnant and provided a sacrifice even for their breach of faith (v. 19). The chapter does not hide the pain of that obedience, and its ending leaves the reader waiting for something more.

Why it was said. A few thousand families, holding the promise of David’s line in a small Persian province, were being drawn back into the idolatry that had sent their fathers into exile (see the introduction, “The hardest chapter”). They needed to see that they could survive only as the people of the LORD, and that priests and leaders must repent with everyone else.

How the chapter makes its case. A weeping crowd gathers, and Shecaniah, whose own family is on the list, confesses the sin, holds out hope, and proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives (vv. 1–4). The people swear, Ezra fasts through the night, and every exile is summoned (vv. 5–8). In the December rain the assembly hears Ezra’s charge and agrees, asking that the cases be heard properly, town by town; four men oppose it (vv. 9–15). Examiners sit for three months (vv. 16–17). The book ends with the list of the guilty, headed by the high priest’s family and their guilt offering, and a line about the children (vv. 18–44).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. The priests’ ram “for their guilt” (v. 19) is the offering for a breach of faith, one of the sacrifices that pointed to the Servant whose soul would make “an offering for guilt” (Isaiah 53:10). And the need is plain: within a generation the same marriages were back (Nehemiah 13:23–27). Separation could guard a people for a time; it could not change a heart. Christ does what Ezra could not. The Bridegroom takes a bride from the nations, unclean and far off, and instead of putting her away, “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:25–26).

For us. Name your sin plainly, and believe that even now there is hope, because Christ has been offered for it. Then do what obedience requires, carefully and without delay. This chapter is not God’s instruction to Christians married to unbelievers: the apostle tells them to stay, and love (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Even Now There Is Hope for Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Confession joined to hope leads to a covenant of costly obedience. While Ezra prays and weeps before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women and children gathers to him, weeping too (v. 1). Shecaniah, whose own family is among the guilty, names the sin, insists that “even now there is hope for Israel”, and proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives and their children, calling on Ezra to lead (vv. 2–4). Ezra puts the leaders and people under oath and spends the night fasting where no one sees (vv. 5–6). Every exile is summoned to Jerusalem within three days, on pain of losing property and place (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 puts confession and hope in one breath, and repentance needs both: confession without hope becomes despair, and hope without confession becomes presumption. The hope rests on God, not on the reform about to be made; they turn back because he is still the God who kept a remnant for himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's night without bread or water is Moses' fast after the golden calf: I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed (Deut 9:18). The leader grieves longest for the sin he did not commit, and does it where nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children, gathered to him out of Israel, for the people wept bitterly. And Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: "We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this. Therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Law. Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Ezra prays, the people gather weeping, and one whose own family is guilty confesses the sin, insists there is still hope, and proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives.

A very great assembly. Ezra had called no meeting. He prayed aloud before the temple, and the people came, men, women and children, weeping. A leader’s honest grief over sin frees others to grieve over what they have been pushing out of mind.

Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam. A Jehiel of the sons of Elam appears in the list of offenders (v. 26), very possibly his own father. If so, the man who stood up and named the sin had it in his own family, and he still said “we”.

We have broken faith … but even now there is hope. “Broken faith” is the word for treachery in holy things, the breach that cost Saul his throne (1 Chronicles 10:13) and the last generation its temple (2 Chronicles 36:14). Yet “even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this.” The first real step back toward God always has both in it: admitting that the sin is as bad as it is, and trusting that God is still merciful.

It is your task, and we are with you. The reform was proposed by the people, not imposed on them; Shecaniah asks Ezra to lead what they have already resolved.

Reading this proposal honestly. This proposal is hard to read, and must be read honestly, because a Christian reader may be living inside the very situation it describes. Three things must be said. First, it was about worship, not race (see the note on 9:1–2). Ezra’s prayer has just described the wives’ peoples as “the peoples who practice these abominations” (9:14); Ruth the Moabite, who said “your God my God”, became David’s great-grandmother; and anyone who left the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD was welcome at the Passover (6:21). The danger was households bringing the gods of Canaan into the remnant God had just rescued from exile for that very sin.

It belonged to its moment. Second, a few thousand families, holding the promise of the Messiah’s line in a Persian province, were being drawn back into the idolatry God had exiled them for. Nehemiah later reminded them what such marriages had done to Solomon, beloved of God, whom foreign women made to sin (Nehemiah 13:26).

Not what God asks of Christians. Third, and plainly, it is not what God asks of a Christian today. The apostle Paul answered the question directly: “if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her”, and the same for a wife (1 Corinthians 7:12–13). His reason turns Ezra’s situation inside out: “For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband” (7:14). Holiness now runs from the believer into the home, not uncleanness the other way. A Christian who marries is to marry “only in the Lord” (7:39); a Christian already married to an unbeliever is to stay, and love, and pray, in hope: “how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (7:16).

When the unbeliever leaves, or home is not safe. If the unbelieving partner insists on leaving, “let it be so”; the believer “is not enslaved” (7:15). That is desertion, and the Westminster Confession of Faith (24.6) and this commentary hold that it frees the believer. No one is asked to stay where they are in danger either: persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, anyone being abused should seek safety at once, and the elders help judge each case.

What happened to the wives and children (v. 44)? The text is silent. Most likely they returned to their own families, perhaps with the certificate the law provided to protect a sent-away wife (Deuteronomy 24:1). Silence is no licence to imagine they were abandoned, nor to pretend it did not hurt.

For anyone once sent away. Anyone once sent away, by a parent who left or a spouse who walked out, may find this chapter hard, and need not pretend otherwise; the Bible records this pain without calling it nothing. And the One this book waits for has said of everyone who comes to him: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). No child of a broken home and no wife put away is outside that promise.

Where Christians differ. Was the sending away cruel, and did God approve it? Some think Ezra overreached: the law forbade making such marriages (Deuteronomy 7:3) but did not command dissolving them, and Malachi says God hates divorce (Malachi 2:16; that is the NKJV’s wording, and the KJV’s “he hateth putting away” says the same, while the ESV renders the difficult Hebrew as a rebuke of the man who does not love his wife but divorces her). Others answer that Malachi condemns men who divorced their covenant wives to marry pagans (Malachi 2:11, 14), while these marriages had been made in defiance of the covenant, with women who worshipped other gods; and the narrator presents the reform as the repentance of a community close to losing its faith, and records no rebuke.

This commentary’s view. The likeliest reading is that the reform was right in that unique moment, when the survival of God’s people and the line of the promise were at stake, and that it is no pattern for Christians (see above).

Uncertain wording. “According to the counsel of my lord” (v. 3): the Hebrew can be read “my lord”, meaning Ezra, or “the Lord”, meaning God; the difference lies only in vowels written into the text centuries later. “My lord” suits the setting, since Shecaniah is addressing Ezra. Either way the covenant was to be made “according to the Law”.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ezra arose and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath that they would do as had been said. So they took the oath. Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and went to the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib, where he spent the night, neither eating bread nor drinking water, for he was mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles. And a proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the returned exiles that they should assemble at Jerusalem, and that if anyone did not come within three days, by order of the officials and the elders all his property should be forfeited, and he himself banned from the congregation of the exiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra binds the people by oath, grieves alone through the night, and the whole community is summoned.

So they took the oath. An oath taken while people see clearly holds them to it later, when they are tempted to think again.

Where he spent the night. The public business done, Ezra could have gone home satisfied. Instead he went into a side room and fasted through the night, “mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles”. (Some scholars use the name of the room’s owner, Jehohanan son of Eliashib, to date Ezra after Nehemiah, but the names were common and the point is uncertain; see the introduction.)

All his property should be forfeited. The summons is severe: anyone who stays away forfeits his property and is cut off from the congregation. At stake was whether the community would remain the people of God at all. The officials had the authority: Artaxerxes’ letter had empowered Ezra to punish anyone who would not obey “the law of your God and the law of the king”, whether by banishment or by confiscation of his goods (7:26). The Hebrew for “forfeited” is the word for something devoted to God, so the property would probably have gone to the temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Trembling Because of This Matter and Because of the Heavy Rain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Serious sin in a community is dealt with by careful process, not by a mob. The men of Judah and Benjamin sit in the open square in the December rain, trembling at the matter and at the weather (v. 9). Ezra charges them plainly: confess to the LORD and do his will (vv. 10–11). They agree, but wisely ask for time, for local elders and judges, and for the cases to be heard town by town (vv. 12–14). Four men oppose it, and they are named but not condemned (v. 15). Named heads of families examine the cases for three months and finish a year to the day after Ezra set out from Babylon (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform is done by careful process, not by a mob. A proposal from the people, an oath, a public assembly, a considered delay, local elders and judges, named examiners, and three months of case after case. Serious sin in a community is not dealt with in an afternoon, and the book shows the patience as well as the resolve.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 records dissent and does not explain it. The Bible does not pretend that the people of God were unanimous about the most painful decision they made.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled at Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. And all the people sat in the open square before the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain. And Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, "You have broken faith and married foreign women, and so increased the guilt of Israel. Now then make confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers and do his will. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the winter rain Ezra names the people’s sin plainly and calls them to confess it to the LORD, then do his will.

Because of the heavy rain. The twentieth day of the ninth month, Chislev, was probably in December, when the winter rains have set in (see the Jewish calendar), and the text is honest about why they were shaking: “because of this matter and because of the heavy rain.” Part of it was conviction and part of it was cold: even in a solemn hour God’s people have bodies.

You have broken faith. In his prayer Ezra had said “we”. Now, speaking to the people, he says “you”. Both are right: before God the leader stands inside the people’s sin; before the people he must name it without softening it.

Make confession to the LORD. The Hebrew is surprising: literally “give thanks” or “give praise” to the LORD. Joshua used the same word with Achan: “give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done” (Joshua 7:19). To confess is not to punish yourself until you feel bad enough. It is to give God the glory of being right about you, and to stop defending yourself.

And do his will. Confession first, then obedience: the order still holds. We confess to a God who has already provided a sacrifice for this very sin (v. 19), and for a Christian that sacrifice is Christ. We are not accepted because we obey, but through what he has done, and therefore we obey; his perfect obedience is counted as ours where ours falls short, and our turning from sin is itself his Spirit’s work in us (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Once Christ has carried the guilt there is nothing left to protect, and “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9): just, because the debt has been paid.

Why confession is hard. We quietly rest our standing with God on our record, so every sin admitted feels like a threat, and we explain it, shrink it, or blame the rain. This week, name one sin to God plainly, with no “but” on the end; and if it hurt someone, tell them too. See also Confession in the Theological Dictionary.
verseByVerse.note: The ninth month (November–December) is the rainy season.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the assembly answered with a loud voice, "It is so; we must do as you have said. But the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open. Nor is this a task for one day or for two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter. Let our officials stand for the whole assembly. Let all in our cities who have taken foreign wives come at appointed times, and with them the elders and judges of every city, until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us." Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people agree to obey, and wisely ask for time and proper hearings; the few who dissent are named but not condemned.

It is so; we must do as you have said. Wet, cold and convicted, they agree, and in the same breath ask for time and for local elders and judges: not evasion but wisdom. Every case involved a household, a wife, very often children, property, and a town where everyone knew everyone. Cases like that cannot be settled by a crowd’s shout in a rainstorm.

Only Jonathan and Jahzeiah opposed this. The four who opposed are named but not explained. Perhaps they thought the delay too long, or the whole measure too hard. The narrator neither condemns nor excuses them. A Shabbethai is among the Levites who, years later, helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it (Nehemiah 8:7). If it is the same man, dissent on one hard question did not remove him from the ministry of the word.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 says literally that these men “stood against” or “stood over” this matter. The ESV and most modern translations read opposition; some older ones, such as the King James Version, read that they were put in charge of it. The word “only” suits opposition better, but it is not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the returned exiles did so. Ezra the priest selected men, heads of fathers' houses, according to their fathers' houses, each of them designated by name. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to examine the matter; and by the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Named heads of families examine the cases one by one for three months, and finish a year to the day after Ezra set out.

Each of them designated by name. Not panic or rumour, but known people taking the time each case required, as hard matters in a church still should be.

By the first day of the first month. They finished a year to the day after Ezra left Babylon (7:9). The hardest part of his commission was complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–44 — All These Had Married Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No house was too near the altar to need repentance, and even for priests there was a sacrifice. The list begins with the sons of Jeshua the high priest and the other priestly houses, who pledge to put away their wives and bring a ram for their guilt (vv. 18–22). Levites, a singer and gatekeepers follow (vv. 23–24), then eighty-four laymen, family by family, nearly all from families in the register of chapter 2 (vv. 25–43). A hundred and eleven men are named in all. The book ends with no celebration, only a line about the children (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: The four priestly families on this list (Jeshua, Immer, Harim, Pashhur) are the four that came home in chapter 2 (2:36-39). Not one priestly house was untouched, and the high priest's own family heads the list. Yet even for them there was an offering (v. 19).
verseByVerse.examples: The book ends with the children and says no more about them. That silence is honest, and the note on v. 44 reads it with the New Testament open.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were found some of the sons of the priests who had married foreign women: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah, some of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers. They pledged themselves to put away their wives, and their guilt offering was a ram of the flock for their guilt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of the guilty begins with the high priest’s family, who pledge to put away their wives and bring the law’s offering for a breach of faith.

Some of the sons of the priests. The list begins at the top. Jeshua the son of Jozadak is the high priest who built the altar (3:2), whom Zechariah saw before the angel in filthy garments (Zechariah 3:3). Two generations later his descendants head the list of the guilty. No house in Israel was too close to the altar to need repentance.

They pledged themselves. Literally, they “gave their hand”: a solemn, public pledge.

Their guilt offering was a ram. The offering is exact: the ram Leviticus prescribes for a breach of faith in the holy things of the LORD (Leviticus 5:15). Breach of faith is the very charge Shecaniah and Ezra had made (vv. 2, 10). The altar built before the temple in chapter 3 was doing what it was built for. There was a sacrifice even for this.

The removal it pointed to. In Zechariah’s vision the filthy garments came off, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you” (Zechariah 3:4), with a promise: “I will bring my servant the Branch” (Zechariah 3:8). The ram was a sign of that greater removal, made once for all when the Servant made “an offering for guilt” (Isaiah 53:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah. Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah. Of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. Of the singers: Eliashib. Of the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every order of the temple’s servants is named among the guilty, yet two of these Levites may later have taught the law.

Of the sons of Immer. The other priestly houses follow, seventeen priests in all, then six Levites, one singer and three gatekeepers.

Kelaiah (that is, Kelita) and Jozabad. Two of the Levite names should be held onto: Kelaiah, whose other name the narrator stops to give, and Jozabad. When Ezra later read the law to the whole city, the Levites who “helped the people to understand the Law” included a Jozabad and a Kelita (Nehemiah 8:7). If they are the same men, two Levites who put away their wives that December became, a dozen years on, teachers of the book that had convicted them. Forgiven men make the most careful teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Israel: of the sons of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Hashabiah, and Benaiah. Of the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah. Of the sons of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. Of the sons of Bebai were Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai. Of the sons of Bani were Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth. Of the sons of Pahath-moab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh. Of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon, Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah. Of the sons of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei. Of the sons of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel, Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi, Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu. Of the sons of Binnui: Shimei, Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah, Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai, Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah, Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph. Of the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jaddai, Joel, and Benaiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighty-four laymen from the leading families are named, family by family: the grandsons of those who first came home.

And of Israel. Seven of the sons of Parosh, six of Elam, six of Zattu, four of Bebai, six of Bani, eight of Pahath-moab, eight of Harim, seven of Hashum, twelve more of Bani, thirteen of Binnui, seven of Nebo. Eighty-four men in eleven family groups.

Familiar family names. Almost every family name here is in the register of chapter 2, several in Ezra’s list in chapter 8: these were the grandsons of the people who wept and shouted over the foundation (3:12–13).

A small number, not a small matter. The whole list comes to a hundred and eleven men: a small number out of tens of thousands, but not a small matter, because priests, Levites and the heads of the leading families set the direction for everyone else.

Why every name is kept. The Bible keeps every name, not to shame men who had confessed and brought their offering, but because God deals with people one by one, and a list of the forgiven is still a list of his own people.

Uncertain wording. The count of a hundred and eleven follows the ESV in verses 37–38. The Hebrew runs on as a list, “and Bani, and Binnui, Shimei”, and it is not certain whether Bani and Binnui are two more men, as the King James Version takes them (making a hundred and thirteen), or the heading of a new family, as the ESV does.

verseByVerse.quote: All these had married foreign women, and some of the women had even borne children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book ends not with a feast but with a line about the children, honest about the cost of reform and leaving the reader waiting for a better answer.

A list and a line. There the book ends: no feast, no dedication, no summary. It is an uncomfortable ending, and it is meant to be. There were women and children in these homes, and the book does not tell us where they went or how they lived. Reform in that hour was real, and it was painful, and Scripture records the pain without pretending it away.

Reading it with the New Testament open. The apostle’s word to a believer married to an unbeliever is the opposite of this chapter’s covenant (see the note on vv. 1–4), and the children of such a home are not to be sent away: “as it is, they are holy” (1 Corinthians 7:14). They are set apart by a believing parent’s teaching and prayers, though each must still come to Christ by his own faith. What changed between Ezra and Paul was not that God grew less holy. It was that the Holy One himself had come, and holiness now spreads outward from those who belong to him.

Brought near by the blood of Christ. The book that ends with foreign wives sent away is followed, in the fullness of time, by a gospel that brings the foreigners in: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ … So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:13, 19). It does this not by lowering the standard of holiness in this chapter, which has never been lowered, but through Christ, the Bridegroom who took a bride from among the nations, unclean and far off, and instead of putting her away, “gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:25–26). Ezra’s community could keep itself holy only by sending the foreigner away. Christ makes the foreigner holy and keeps her.

Where Christians differ. What does Paul mean by calling the children of such a home “holy” (1 Corinthians 7:14)? Paedobaptist brothers read it as a mark of covenant membership.

This commentary’s view. With the 1689 London Baptist Confession, this commentary reads it as the influence of a believing home, and gladly owns that faithful Christians differ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 44 is difficult, and its last clause is uncertain. The ESV reads “some of the women had even borne children”; 1 Esdras, a later Greek retelling, reads that they sent the women away with their children. Either way the verse names the children, and says no more.

10.theology:
Shecaniah's even now there is hope (v. 2) holds together what repentance needs: an honest name for the sin and a settled confidence in God's mercy. The guilt offering of v. 19 shows that the hope was not presumption.

The chapter belongs to a unique moment, when a tiny remnant carrying the promise of the Messiah's line was being drawn back into the idolatry it had been exiled for; Malachi condemns the same sin in the same generation (Mal 2:11). The new covenant reverses the direction of the danger: holiness now flows from the believer into the marriage (1 Cor 7:14), and Christ brings the foreigner near (Eph 2:13) and makes his bride holy rather than putting her away (Eph 5:25-27).
10.examples:
The man who first named the sin came from a family on the list, and he still said we. The people who proposed the reform also asked that it be done properly, case by case, and four dissenters are named without being condemned.

The high priest's family is first on the list, yet two Levites on it may be the same men who later helped the whole city understand the law. Confessed sin did not end their usefulness.

keyVerse.quote: We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the chapter and the book’s last word of hope. Shecaniah names the sin without softening it and in the same breath refuses to despair, because Israel’s hope never rested on its record but on the God who had kept a remnant for himself. That is the shape of every true repentance, and for those who turn back to God through Christ, “even now” is always true.

10.reflection:
Shecaniah said in one breath “we have broken faith” and “even now there is hope” (v. 2). Why does real repentance need both, and which do you find harder to hold on to?

The people asked for the cases to be heard carefully, town by town, with local elders and judges (vv. 13–14). What can a church learn here about handling serious sin without either ignoring it or acting in haste?

Two Levites named among the guilty may later have helped the people understand the law (v. 23; Nehemiah 8:7). How does the gospel give hope to people whose failures are publicly known, including you?

Ezra’s community could keep itself holy only by sending the foreigner away; Christ makes his bride holy and keeps her (Ephesians 5:25–27). How does this change the way you think about your own belonging to God, and about the people your church welcomes?
